maintopic: DEATH OF MR. A. B. HUNT, M.P.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. A. B. HUNT, M.P.
speechtext:
Hon. members of the
House will have learned with feelings of sorrow and great regret of the death at eight o'clock this morning, at the Ottawa Civic Hospital, of one of our number, Mr. Aylmer Byron Hunt, member for the constituency of Compton in the province of Quebec. During the last year or two Mr. Hunt has been in ill-health, having had to undergo several opera-ations. He has, however, been regularly in attendance throughout the present session and was in his seat in parliament as recently as ten days ago, at which time he went to the hospital in order to undergo another operation. His impaired strength and vitality were unequal to the tax which the operation placed upon them, and I am informed, he died this morning from its effects.
Mr. Hunt was in his sixty-first year. In point of service he was one of the oldest representatives in the Commons. He entered parliament over twenty years ago, having been first returned as the member for Compton in the general elections of 1904. He continued to represent that constituency in all subsequent parliaments, save the one following the general elections of 1911, when he met defeat by a slender majority. At the last general election he was returned by a majority of something like 4,000.
Mr. Hunt was closely identified with the farming and commercial interests of the county he represented in parliament. Like many another hon. member of this House, he, in his younger years, took an active interest in municipal affairs, and was honoured by being elected mayor of the town of Bury in which he was born, and subsequently by being chosen warden of the county. In 1900, following in the steps

Deceased Member-Mr. Hunt
of his father who in the year preceding had represented the county of Compton in the Provincial Legislature of Quebec, he contested the riding in the Liberal interests. Though unsuccessful in this contest his popularity was such that he was chosen as the Liberal candidate in the federal elections of 1904, when, as mentioned, he was first returned to this parliament.
Just how significant was the part played by Mr. Hunt in the politics of the Eastern Townships and how considerable the measure of public confidence he enjoyed, may be gauged from the circumstance that it was in the general elections of 1904 that the county 6f Compton for the first time since the days of Confederation changed its representation from Conservative to Liberal; also by the fact that the majorities obtained by Mr. Hunt in the elections of 1919 and 1921 were the largest federal majorities ever given in the history of the county.
Mr. Hunt possessed the characteristics and qualities which inspire confidence and trust, qualities which in public life add to the number of a man's friends and leave him without enemies when his day's work is done. He was quiet and reserved in demeanour, genuinely sympathetic and public-spirited, loyal and steadfast in all the relationships of life. In these many relationships he will be greatly missed. Especially will his loss be felt by hon. members on this side and in the country by the Liberal party to whose principles he was so true, and of which he was so devoted a supporter. We in the House of Commons, who knew him best will greatly miss his kindly and cheerful personality. Our sympathy will go out at this time to the constituency which Mr. Hunt represented, in the loss of their member, and especially to Mrs. Hunt and to her sons and daughters in the overwhelming bereavement they have so suddenly sustained. I know that I express the common sentiment and desire of all here assembled in requesting, Mr. Speaker, that you convey to Mrs. Hunt and to the members of her family t'he heartfelt sympathy of all hon. members of this House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. A. B. HUNT, M.P.
speechtext:
Once again parliament is
called on by the intervention of death to lament the loss of one of our members, and to pay to his memory a tribute of honour and respect. As the Prime Minister has said, Mr. Hunt was one of the oldest of our number in point of service in this House. He devoted most of his life to the public service, but throughout that period maintained an atti-

tude of quiet reserve and unobtrusiveness which made him not so well known among all the members of the House as otherwise would have been his fortune. With us on this side he mingled little, but was known to all as a devoted friend of his country, as a cheerful, good companion, and a faithful public servant. He did all that man could do within his means and capacity. He served his country ably. He took part in very many business activities, and was connected with much that was of advantage to his people, and served in every way with fidelity and with ability. His family is large and in that manner also he leaves behind him an inheritance for his country, the value of which we all appreciate. I am sure that hon. members on this side of the House for whom I speak desire permission to join in this tribute of respect to his memory, and we ask also to be allowed to unite with hon. members opposite in the message which you, Mr. Speaker, are requested to send to his widow and his family.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. A. B. HUNT, M.P.
speechtext:
On
behalf of the hon. members who sit in this part of the House, I should like to say that it was with deep sorrow and regret that we learned this morning of the death of Mr. Hunt. Though, as has already been stated, he did not take a prominent part in the debates of this House, yet I am sure he was respected by every hon. member. Manifestly he has been appreciated and respected by his constituents as shown by the long term during which he represented them in this chamber. He has served them honourably and well. I can only ask that our sympathy be expressed to those near and dear to him for the great loss which they have sustained in the death of husband and father.

speechtext:
As requested
by the leaders of all parties in this House, I shall forward to the widow and relatives of the late Mr. Hunt tributes of sympathy which have been expressed for them in their bereavement.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient that more effective consideration and recognition be given to the resolution adopted by parliament on March 12, 1923, recognizing the priority of the Hudson Bay railway, with reference to other transportation projects started subsequently.
He said: This matter has been before the House on a number of occasions, and in bringing it forward again I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that those of us who are interested in the Hudson Bay railway will offer no apology for discussing the subject. Wle who are pressing for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway balieve implicitly in the feasibility and in the future success of that project and in that conviction we have no need to fee! apologetic. We represent hundreds of thousands of people in the west who to-day are equally confident of the feasibility and the successful operation of this railway; and they believe in it as a possible outlet for their produce and as an inlet for their purchases. These people believe that it would overcome the great handicap under which the west is to-day suffering by reason of high transportation costs. The peop!e whom I represent and among whom I have lived for the last thirty-odd years have great faith in the outcome of the undertaking. Some of these people have entered Canada by this route, while others have worked on the railway as well as on the terminals, so that they are intimately associated with the whole thing and know whereof they speak. And it is because of this intimate knowledge of the Hudson bay proposition that they believe so firmly in its ultimate success if the work is carried to completion.
The people of the west, however, believe in the justice of completing the Hudson Bay railway; and more than that, they believe in the righteousness of it, if I may put it that way: many of them believe that the Hudson bay was placed as it is by an all-wise Creator for the purpose of serving as an outlet for the great agricultural plateau of the middle west. The people in that part of the country are of the opinion that it would do more towards bettering conditions in the west if this railway were completed, than any other transportation project could accomplish. The result of all this is that those who inhabit the three prairie provinces are practically a unit in their request for the im-

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Knox
mediate completion of the Hudson Bay railway; and requests come from organizations representing every phase of western activity -from our legislatures down through our farmers' organizations, our labour bodies and our boards of trade. I have here a copy of a resolution passed by the United Farmers of Alberta which I shall read to the House. It has been suggested on former occasions that the province of Alberta was not very strong in its attitude towards the railway; but the following resolution would not be passed by the organization to which I have referred- which certainly represents the thought of Alberta-if the province did not favour the completion of the road. The resolution reads:
Resolved that we go on record as being strongly in favour of the early completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
This was adopted in January last. The thought has occurred to me that it is rather a strange situation that the people of the prairie provinces, living in close proximity to the Hudson Bay railway and having every reason to know something about the matter, should be almost unanimously in favour of its completion, while people living at a remote distance who naturally, one would think, would not be expected to know so much about it, are very largely opposed to the undertaking. I have in mind the section of the east particularly centering around Montreal. We in the west feel that this opposition is not justified; we look on Hudson bay as our natural outlet, and we feel that we have contributed to the expenses of this project up to the present time, besides possibly having something left over from the sale of some of the western lands.
As to the history of the Hudson Bay railway undertaking itself, I shall be very brief. This matter has been a source of agitation on the part of the west for the last forty years or more. The railway was first begun by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1910 and the work was carried on by the govern-' ment of Sir Robert Borden, closing down in 1918 without any apparent reason, after there had been spent on the railway and the terminals some $21,000,000. The total length of the line is 424 miles, and! this has all been graded; the steel has been laid on 332 miles, all the bridges having been built. It will be seen from this that only a distance of 92 miles remains to be laid with steel, and it is hard to understand why this stretch has not been completed after the construction has got to that stage.
A number of hon. gentlemen sitting around me have made personal trips of inspection

to the bay and no doubt they will tell the House what they have found on these trips. I have not personally visited the locality, although I hope to do so some time in the future. But those who have made the trip report that the work already done is still Standing up well and is in good condition. Since these trips were made it has been reported through the press that as the result of a very severe storm that swept over Hudson bay a good deal of damage was done; and I have been informed by people who think they ought to know that sections of the bridging laid over to the artificial island in the harbour have been carried away. In consequence of this information I made a point of consulting the chief engineer, Mr. McLachlan, this morning; I asked him what the reports showed in regard to this alleged damage, and he assured me that the bridge is standing there in perfect condition, no damage having been done, except for the fact that much of the gravel which had been placed on the piers when work ceased, has been swept away. He tells me too that some of the barges and dredges were swept from their moorings. The House will of course readily understand that as there was no protection from the storm it was only to be expected that to this limited extent some injury would be caused by so severe a storm. Some of these barges were carried across the estuary and stranded on the other side; but the engineer assures me that no great damage has been done, the work still standing secure. This information was very reassuring after the reports that had gone out through the press, as it is just possible that some one may see fit during the debate to-day to mention this storm. I had an opportunity of discussing the storm with an officer of the Hudson's Bay Company who is in charge of a post in the northwest extremity of the bay. He assured me that it was of extreme severity. In fact he said that the oldest Eskimos had no remembrance of anything like it ever having happened before. Port Nelson having in its present unprotected condition come through that severe storm without any serious damage to the uncompleted works there, I do not think we have much to fear on this head. It is significant that this storm happened in November, which is one of the months w'hen opponents of the scheme tell us the bay and port are frozen solid. I think we now have sufficient proof to the contrary.
On March 12, 1923, Mr. Speaker, I moved the following resolution:

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Knox
That in the opinion of this House, the government of Canada give further consideration to the report of the Senate committee on the Hudson Bay railway with a view to safeguarding the investment of public moneys made in the construction of that portion of the work completed to date, and that the government recognize the priority of this undertaking with reference to other transportation projects started subsequent to the Hudson Bay railway.
I would point out that after considerable discussion this resolution was adopted by the House. Although so adopted, and therefore representing the decision of this House two years ago, it is significant that no effort has yet been made to give this transportation project priority over other transportation projects started subsequently. Some work was done in the summers of 1923 and 1924 to rehabilitate the portion of the road over which trains run. An estimate of $350,000 was voted in 1924; another $300,000 had been voted in 1923, but only some S60,000 odd was spent in that year. So that altogether during those two years only about $413,000 was spent in an effort to rehabilitate that portion of the road over which trains are run. During that time the money spent, for instance, on the Welland canal, has run into millions of dollars. I might say that the Welland canal was started subsequent to the Hudson Bay project. In 1923 a vote of $11,800,000 and in 1924 a further vote of $11,000,000 was passed for the prosecution of work on this canal, making a total for those two years of $22,800,000 as compared with the $413,000 spent on the Hudson Bay project. This year I find in the estimates an item of $15,000,000 for the Welland canal. As yet we have no intimation of what supplementary estimate will be brought down for the Hudson Bay railway, but if it is to have any priority over the Welland cana'l project, this estimate should surely be for a sum sufficient to complete the work. I would impress on the House that the resolution passed in 1923 has not been observed by the government; certainly no priority has been given to the Hudson Bay railway.
Is it any wonder that there is a feeling of distrust, suspicion and disappointment in the prairie provinces on this matter? We in the west are suffering more or less by the discrimination-if I might use that term- against us in respect of the customs tariff, and it is bearing heavily upon us. But when it comes to a refusal by a certain portion of eastern Canada to permit the completion of a project, the funds for which were raised by the sale of western lands, then, Mr. Speaker, we certainly feel like crying "How long, O Lord, how long!" This project was supported and endorsed by both the old political parties, parliament has sanctioned it time and again, settlers have gone into that country on the distinct understanding that the Hudson Bay railway would be completed, and those already there have extended their operations and investments on the strength of the repeated promises that the line would be built through to the bay. Evidently these people had greater faith in the governments of that time than they could be expected to have in the government of to-day.
It has been said that the Hudson Bay railway is the child of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). Undoubtedly he turned the first sod, thus giving the project his blessing and, I have no doubt, his sympathy. I do not think that to-day down in his heart he has changed one particle, but it is impossible for him to carry the project through without the support of his colleagues in the cabinet, which evidently he has not got. As I said a few days ago when speaking on the budget, at one time we had great expectations of assistance from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). While speak* ing on this subject in the West during the recess he certainly gave us to understand tha* he was an out and out supporter of the completion of the railway, and the west was looking forward to something being done this session through the efforts that he was likely to put forth to assist us in getting the project completed. But we got a rude shock a few days ago when, in his speech on the budget, he showed that he had changed his attitude somewhat, because instead of urging the immediate completion of the road he advocated a further investigation as to which was the better terminal. Port Nelson or Fort Churchill. As I said at the time, it looked to me very much like drawing a red herring across the trail-in other words, another excuse for further delay.
Now, Sir, if the government wish to retain, or possibly I should use the word obtain, the respect and confidence of the west, my suggestion and advice to them would be to consider what we are up against in regard to the customs tariff, and also what we are up against in regard to our transportation problems. Apparently the government could not see their way to give us any consideration when framing their budget, but they still have another opportunity to partially set themselves right with the west, and my proposal is that to this end they take half of the $15,000,000 which appears in the estimates for the Welland canal and apply the money to the Hudson Bay project, for this amount would be far

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Knox
more than sufficient to bring it to the stage where it could function successfully. By so doing they would help allay the present distrust of our people in the west and forever end this annual controversy.
I have here a copy of a letter which I would like to read to the House. It is from Mr. 0. D. Hill, of Melfort, Saskatchewan, in my constituency, wTho made a trip up to the bay last summer. I should have referred to this letter earlier in my remarks, but I will put it in now, as it gives an idea of what the condition of the road is. He says:
I was out to Port Nelson this summer in company with Colonel James of Regina, and both of us came back far more enthused over the project than ever. I am sending you, under separate cover, some pictures taken of the road. We were agreeably surprised with the condition of thp roadbed. And I make this statement without fear of contradiction, having been over every transcontinental road in Canada and over some in the United States, that there isn't a natural roadbed in North America that can compare with that of the Hudson Bay railroad.
There are stretches of this road running for miles and miles in a straight line where there is very little dump at all, the land being so level that there is only ballast underneath the rails. Some of the pictures that I am enclosing will corroborate this. When you consider this and the fact that the heaviest gradient is only four-tenths of one per cent, that there are no long fills, or long cuts, it would make you think that Providence had provided this natural way to the sea. Any gradients are in favor of the out-going traffic, which will be the heavier for a long time. There is nothing on the road which would approach my conception of a muskeg. The road for the whole way is on solid ground. There is no place where there is any mud or water coming up through the ties. The longest dump is at Armstrong lake and it is wonderful the state of preservation that this is in.
The road from Le Pas to Mile 214 has had a considerable amount of work done on it this summer. One of the pictures which I am enclosing shows this, where the ties are taken up and put out on the side cut, and is	as good	as	any branch	line	in the west.The road from 214	to	332, which is	the	second crossing of the	Nelson,	it	is estimated	by	a competentman, can be rehabilitated for half a million dollars. It is only	natural	to	think that	this portion of
the road, which has had nothing done on it for eight or nine years, should be considerably damaged by the elements, but this has nothing to do with the roadbed.
From 332 through to Port Nelson the dump is all complete and whilst we only saw both ends of it, we have spoken to men who have gone over the whole dump and they claim that it is just as good on the average over the whole grade as at the ends and we should say from this that there is very little which has to be done with the dump before the steel could ~be laid on it.
I am safe in saying that any loyal, reasonable unprejudiced citizen of Canada, come from where he may, taking the trip over the road to the bay as I did, could not help but become an enthusiastic supporter of the project.
I have no wish to speak at any great length on this matter, because it has been put before the House so often that to do so would be to repeat what has already been

said. My object is to draw to the attention of the House and particularly of the government, the fact that they have 4 p.m. not carried out the wishes of parliament as indicated by the adoption of that resolution on March 12, 1923, in regard to giving the Hudson Bay railway priority over other transportation projects started subsequently. I ask the government to give us some reasonable assurance that steps will be taken to carry the expressed wishes of parliament into effect.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want, if I may, to congratulate the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) upon having again introduced a resolution dealing specifically with the Hudson Bay railway project, with due insistence upon its priority as a national undertaking. I cannot hope to add to the information already available on this subject, information which is very complete and easily accessible. It is not my desire unduly to prolong the debate, but in view of the fact that I visited Port Nelson last autumn, it occurred to me that it might be interesting and not wholly unprofitable if I were to convey to the House in a few sentences the impressions made upon my mind by what I saw and experienced in the northland.
The party of which I was a member left the Pas on the 28th of August last. We went north actuated by-shall I say?-a two-fold desire. The first was a desire to determine for ourselves the actual condition of the roadbed already constructed. There were those who contended that the road was in an excellent state of preservation, and there were others-pessimists of course-who informed us prior to our departure that the roadbed had long since disappeared into the muskegs; that only the tops of the telegraph poles were visible, and that even they were covered with snow for at least eleven months out of twelve. We wanted to determine for ourselves just what the actual conditions were. In the second place we wanted to determine, so far as amateurs could determine, what the facilities were at Port Nelson for the loading and unloading of cargoes. We decided to travel the 332 miles from the Pas to Kettle rapids by open gas car, in order that our inspection might be intimate, thorough, and satisfactory in every sense. It enabled Premier Bracken, who is a scientific agriculturist, to make soil tests on the way up and also to interview the many settlers and to inspect their gardens, in which we found vegetables and grains growing abundantly.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hoey
With respect to the condition of the road,
I think I can make this statement without fear of contradiction that the first 100 miles is in my judgment in as good condition at the moment as any branch line in the Dominion of Canada over which I have travelled. The territory itself is monotonously level and prairie-like. At Herb lake, 12 miles west of mile 81, there is a village, which we visited, of about 300 people who have gone in there awaiting the completion of the road, but who in the meantime are doing all they possibly can to develop the country. From mile 100 to mile 214 the roadbed was in process of reconstruction at the time of our visit. Old ties were being replaced with new ones; rails were being straightened; gravel trains were travelling to and fro supplying ballast; so that by this time the road up to mile 214 is in splendid condition for heavy traffic. From mile 214 to mile 332, where the road crosses the Nelson river for the second time, it is not in an ideal condition, and one could hardly expect it would be. We encountered, however, only one washout. Hon. members will realize the condition of that part of the road when I tell them that we travelled over it in an open gas car at a rate of 30 miles an hour without any mishap and without any serious inconvenience.
We went from Kettle rapids to Port Nelson by canoe. One could not but be profoundly impressed by the turbulent and swift-flowing waters of the Nelson river. The Nelson river is one of the great rivers of the world; it drains more territory than any other river of which we have any knowledge anywhere, and is capable of developing three million horsepower of electrical energy. It took us exactly two days to make the trip from Kettle rapids to Flamborough Bead. There we left our canoes and waited the outgoing tide that was to take us down to Port Nelson harbour itself. While at Flamborough Head we could not resist the temptation-although it was the first week in September-in view of the absence of ice and snow, to bathe in the tide water, remaining in about thirty minutes and enjoying a very refreshing swim.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Only an Irishman would
enjoy that.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
There were, unfortunately or
fortunately, three of us, two native bom Canadians and one Irishman. It is difficult for me to convey to the House the sensations that passed through me as I stood in that northern tide water. I could not
help but think of the words written across the front entrance to this building:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
Standing there I asked myself, why was this northern sea, with its stories of heroism, perhaps the most wholesome of them all-why was it overlooked, nay forgotten? And standing there I suggested to my associates that the words be changed to read something like this:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
North, east and west this giant state.
That may not be good poetry, but it expressed to me on that occasion a great soulstirring-shall I say? ennobling-truth. We drifted down from Flamborough Head to Port Nelson itself on the outgoing tide, and the first impression made upon my mind was profoundly disappointing. It is not a harbour, it is rather a roadstead. It is V-shaped, narrow to the south and wide toward the north. It is exposed to the northern storms; and I was of the opinion when I gazed upon it at first that no steamer could lie side by side at the artificial island without being seriously disturbed by the violence of the storms. The artificial island which is constructed there-at least the half-mile which is constructed-is about five hundred feet wide, and it is connected with the shore by a bridge of seventeen spans of two hundred feet each, or approximately so, with the cribwork. We walked over that and inspected the island. Then one of my associates pointed to two ships, two derelicts, the appearance and presence of which changed my opinion somewhat-one about two miles south of the artificial island, or approximately so, and the other about two miles north. Both, I understand, were beached about the year 1913, and these ships to-day are just as symmetrical, both as upright and in almost as good a state of preservation, as if they were wrecked yesterday; and I expressed the belief that if those ships had been beached, say, on the Antrim coast, or some other coast I had previously visited during my brief career, they would have been smashed into matchwood in less than three months. The fact of importance is that the violence of any storm there has long since spent itself before it reaches the harbour of Nelson at all, so that ships lying parallel with the artificial island and in harmony with the current are perfectly safe. In this connection I want to read just a brief excerpt from the evidence given by Mr. McLachlan before the Senate committee:

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hoey
A ship in going from deep water to Hudson bay must weather any storms that may come during her stay at Port Nelson while tied to the wharf, but the 20 miles of relatively shallow water from deep water to the port cause the deep sea rolls or waves to be broken uip, and while serious so far as small light vessels were concerned, would not affect a large vessel.
Now you may ask: What did you see at Port Nelson apart from the artificial island and the bridge? I think I could answer that question more intelligent'y if I were asked what did I not see? Because I saw almost everything except people; there are very few people there. I have heard during the last few days that the reason why the Minister of Agriculture did not make the complete trip on the occasion of his visit that they could not assure him there would be an audience at Port Nelson when he arrived there before which he could display his undoubted oratorical powers. They have at Port Nelson a dry dock two hundred feet long and forty-six feet wide. They have there also almost everything necessary for the maintenance of an up-to-date construction camp. They have a wireless station there which has been dismantled, but the equipment of which is in a splendid state of repair. They have six or seven sea-going tugs. They have a Mounted Police station, and I was given to understand that the complete townsite, which is rather an attractive one, is owned wholly and exclusively by the Dominion government, so that whatever may be said for or against Port Nelson no private monopa'y has got a foothold there so far. The people of western Canada-I wish this were given publicity -are not asking to-day for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. That railway is already constructed, not in part but in its entirety, from Hudson Bay junction to tide water at Port Nelson. To ask then for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, in view of the fact that it is already constructed, would be meaningless and absurd.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean that the rails are laid all the way?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
No, I will explain that. What they are asking for is that rails and ties be placed on the ninety-two miles from Kettle rapids to the bay which part of the road is already graded. Now we did not walk on our way back the ninety-two miles from the port to Kettle rapids; the distance was too great. But we did walk five or six miles in an attempt to determine just what condition the grade was in, and we found at in almost perfect shape, some members of the party expressing the belief that it was in as good

shape as during the first month of its construction. There are no more bridges to be constructed. There was one small bridge over the Limestone river, I understand, a wooden structure, which has fallen into a state of dilapidation. This would' have to be repaired. But the great bridges, one over the Saskatchewan at Le Pas, one over the Nelson, at the Mani-tou rapids, one over the Nelson again at Kettle rapids, have all been constructed and are in a splendid state of preservation. You ask what would be my recommendation. My recommendation -with respect to the Hudson Bay railway would be simply this: that the government undertake to lay the rails from Kettle rapids to the bay almost immediately. The rails for 332 miles are 80-pound rails. I think it might be possible to have those rails on the Canadian National roads which are not in operation-if there are such-removed and placed there. Surely that could be done without involving any considerable expense. Yon ask what would be my recommendation in respect to the harbour. I would not at the present time spend any considerable sum at Port Nelson. I would put down the ties and rails and I would say to the owners of the tramp steamers, "Here is an almost unlimited amount of cargo provided you can prove that the navigation of the straits is commercially feasible;" and I would allow the expenditures on Port Nelson to be determined by the amount of trade developed there during the next three or four or ten years. If no trade develops no expenditure will be necessary, I cannot see any reason in the world, in view of the new channel that has been discovered, why tramp steamers could not come in now and unload grain at the artificial island, provided elevators are erected there, and I understand one company has promised, and guaranteed in fact, that they are prepared to go ahead with the erection of an elevator there provided the government lays down the steel to the port itself.

speechtext: Just for information, would the hon. gentleman be willing to tell us what company is willing to build the elevator there?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
In conversation with some of the people at Port Nelson I learned that their attitude towards us when we asked about the frozen nature of the territory was strikingly

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hoey
similar to what our attitude would be if one went down to Kansas City, and were approached there by a resident of that city and asked if it would be safe for a woman to visit the city of Winnipeg in November, or if it would be too cold for her to remain in that city during that period of the year. The questions with respect to the frozen territory and the dreadful storms that attack it are so absurd that the people refuse to answer them and simply smile. They remind us of something that we are too prone to forget, and that is that all the charges directed against that north country were years ago directed against the prairie provinces. I want to read a statement which should be of considerable interest to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and others who come from British Columbia. It was published in London Truth, in 1881, several years before I was born, and re-published in the Manitoba Free Press June 27, 1924. It reads:
The Canadian Dominion Bubble
The article reprinted below appeared under the above heading in the issue of London "Truth", September 1, 1881.
A careful perusal of it is recommended to the various " knockers " of the Hudson bay route resident in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa and elsewhere-not to overlook a few right here in Winnipeg.
Forty years from now their lugubrious predictions about the northern route will read as curiously as this extract of the year 1881 from "Truth", which was then one of the most influential weeklies published in London. The article from "Truth follows:-
"The Canadian Pacific Railroad Company" has begun, I see, to launch its bonds. "A group of Montreal and New York bankers" has undertaken to "float" ten million dollars' worth of the Company's land grant bonds, and the Bank of Montreal, with its usual courage, has taken one-fourth of the entire loan. This announcement looks as if the Canadians were going to raise the necessary capital on the other side of the water, but I have a shrewd suspicion that they have no real intention of doing anything of the kind. The New Yorkers are keen enough gamblers, and reckless enough at times, I admit, and yet it is impossible to believe that they are such fools as to put their money into this mad project. I would as soon credit them with a willingness to subscribe hard cash in support of a scheme for the utilization of icebergs. The Canadian Pacific Railway will run, if it be ever finished, through a country frost-bound for seven or eight months of the year, and will connect with the eastern part of the Dominion a province which embraces about as forbidding country as any on the face of the earth. British Columbians, they say< have forced on the execution of this part of the contract under which they became incorporated with the Dominion, and believe that prosperity will come to them when the line is made. This is a delusion on their part. British Columbia is a barren, cold mountainous country, that is not worth keeping. It would never have been inhabited at all, unless by trappers of the Hudson's Bay Company, had the "gold fever" not taken a party of mining adventurers there; and ever since that fever died down the place has been going from bad to worse, Fifty railways would not galvanise it into prosperity.
Nevertheless the Canadian government has fairly launched into this project, and I have no doubt the
English public will soon be asked to further it with their cash. The parade of selling bonds in New York and Montreal is- the new way of doing business that "syndicates", "bankers", and loan contractors have adopted in order that it may seem that they have faith in the schemes they father. I doubt if ten million dollars of ready cash could be found in all Canada for this or any other work of utility at a pinch; -

Will the hon.
gentleman tell us who is the author of that interesting document, whether it was the late Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, or the late Hon. Edward Blake. It sounds so familiar.

The article is a reprint. It

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Who is the correspondent? How did it come there?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It is an excerpt taken from
London Truth. The name of the correspondent is not given. I am quoting it from a reprint in the Manitoba Free Press. The article continues:
-but the Canadians are not such idiots as to part wiitth one dollar of their own if they can borrow their neighbours'. The Canadians spend money and we provide it. That has been the arrangement hitherto, and it has worked splendidly-for the Canadians-too well for them to try any other plan with a scheme like the Pacific railway, which they must know is never likely to yield a single red cent of interest on the money that may be sunk in it. A friend of mine told me-and he knew what he was talking about-that he did not believe the much-touted Manitoba settlement would hold out many years. The people who have gone there cannot stand the coldness of the winters. Men and cattle are frozen to death in numbers that would rather astonish the intending settler if he knew; and those that are not killed outright are often maimed for life by frostbites. Its street nuisances kill the people with malaria, or drive them mad with plagues of insects; and to keep themselves alive during the long winter they have to (imitate the habits of the Esquimo. Those who want to know what it is like should read the not-yet-forgotten books of Colonel Butler. His "Great Lone Land" is the land of which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has as yet five-and-twenty million acres to sell, and it is through a death-dealing region of this kind that "The new railway is to run."
Might I add to that a statement taken from Stefansson's book, the Northward Course of Empire:
On the basis of reliable testimony which fills a hugh volume, the British committee concluded in substance that the climate of southern Manitoba and the Saskatchewan is unsuitable for colonization by average Europeans and that in such a country no people will live permanently except fur traders because they are eccentric, missionaries because they are self-sacrificing, and Indians because they do not know' any better. But since then there has grown up in the country which was the very centre of all the testimony the city of Winnipeg, with its 300,000 inhabitants, the third largest city in Canada, the Chicago of the Canadian west, and growing as rapidly and substantially as any city in Canada.
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hoey

In January of last year I visited the Prince Albert district, which is one of the most prosperous districts in Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) and myself drove by automobile from his place, which is about eight miles east of the town, into the town every day during the month of January, without any serious inconvenience, and indeed, without any inconvenience at all. Yet, what was said, indeed, what was written from the very site of Prince Albert a few years ago by Sir William Butler? He said:
Those who, in summer or autumn visit the great prairie of the Saskatchewan can form but a faint idea of its winter fierceness and utter desolation. They are prone to paint the scene as wanting only the settler's hut, the yoke of oxen the wagon, to become at once the paradise of the husbandman. They little know of what they speak. Should they really wish to form a true conception of life in these solitudes, let them go out towards the close of November-
November, mind you.
-into the treeless waste; then, midst fierce storm and biting cold, and snowdrift so dense that earth and heaven seem wrapped together in indistinguishable chaos, they will witness a sight as different from their summer ideal as a mid-Atlantic mid-winter storm varies from a tranquil moonlight on the Aegean sea.
Mr. Lonsdale Green, of Chicago, writing to Stefansson, comments on Sir William Butler's report as follows:
Butler was a good writer and the above is a good description, but there is quite a large city right at the place where the above was written and as Sir William died only eleven years ago, he lived to see it.
I look upon the completion of the Hudson Bay railroad, the laying down of ninety-two miles of steel, as the challenge of the northland, that has been misunderstood and vilified by ignorant persons, for due recognition and for an opportunity to make a contribution which it is capable of making to the cause of Canadian development and unity. I look upon the Hudson Bay railway as the challenge of those restless northern tide-waters to the restless and adventurous spirits of this country, to the resourcefulness and enterprise of the Canadian people. If the Hudson Bay railway was being launched to-day, I say frankly that I do not think I could without hesitation endorse it in view of our financial condition. But in view of the fact that this railway is four-fifths completed, why not, by the expenditure of a little more money, make the greatest experiment that has ever been attempted in the history of this country? Speaking for the people of western Canada with whom I am more or less intimately associated, I say that the people of the west are prepared to leave this project in abeyance, provided that the people of Canada are prepared to leave in
[Mr. Hoey.)
abeyance or to set aside other public works for a term of, say five or six years. But the people of western Canada, in their present temper, are not prepared to leave this project in abeyance while we are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars a year on golf courses, while we are making provision for the construction of a second bridge across the St. Lawrence at the city of Montreal. The people of western Canada are not prepared to leave this project in abeyance in view of its history and the promises made, while we continue to spend millions of dollars annually on the Welland canal.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: There are in this chamber still a few men in whom I have confidence, despite the somewhat demoralizing experiences through which we have passed during the last few days. One of the few men in whom I have still a considerable measure of faith is the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He turned the first sod on the Hudson Bay railway. What could be more appropriate than thalt he should drive the last spike? Surely that is a consummation devoutly to be wished. I look forward to his pronouncement on this occasion with considerable confidence. Taking all the facts into consideration and in view of the small expenditure that we are demanding, I hope he will be able on this occasion to make a statement that will encourage the people who have been fighting for the completion of this railway very persistently and, I think, consistently since the work was abandoned.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are again discussing this hardy perennial, the Hudson Bay railway. I rise to make a few remarks on this subject, because I believe it is the greatest economic and fundamental issue facing western Canada. I believe further it is an issue into which the whole future of the confederation of Canada is woven. I think

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward
it was the hen. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who referred some time ago in this House to an address delivered by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) in the city of Brandon. He made some reference to secession. He also referred to another gentleman who had stated that in certain sections of this country, if a plebescite were taken, it woulld be discovered thalt two-thirds of the population would vote for secession. He went on to picture what a horrible thing that wouild be. I wondered at the time if the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River realized to what extent the party to which he belongs is responsible for that very condition. And I say with a great deal of regret that that is absolutely true. There are whole constituencies in western Canada where, if a plebiscite were taken to-morrow, I am convinced that sixty or seventy per cent of the people would vote for secession. That is a most serious state of affairs if we intend to perpetuate the present confederation. But in order to inform ourselves fully as to the cause, the fundamental cause, of this state of mind of the people we must go back at least to the reciprocity pact of 1911.
I believe it was the hon. member for Duf-ferin (Mr. Woods) who referred to a certain caucus he had attended prior to the election of 1911, wherein he told us that the Conservative party of that day had hoisted the British flag to the top of the mast. I want to say to him and to the House that this is exactly what they did not do; probably at no time in the history of the British Empire was that grand old flag of liberty trailed through the filth and mire of the Canadian political slough to a greater extent than in the election of 1911. They pulled the British flag down and wrapped it around Sir Robert Borden; and all the little Bordenites went up and down this country with that flag wrapped about them, declaring that we should have no truck or trade with the Yankees. And so they defeated reciprocity. Then coming down a little further we reach the year 1917; and I would direct this very pointedly to the attention of the ex-Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and his party. They again are very largely responsible for the economic condition which prevails in western Canada as a result of the cessation of the work on the Hudson Bay railway when it was almost completed. Furthermore, I venture to say that not one quarter of one per cent of the people of eastern Canada knew that the work on the Hudson Bay railway had been carried to the stage it had reached; nor do they know, that all the
material was on the ground for its completion, at the time that work was stopped and that the grade had all been built. Those men who now appear to be so solicitous of the economic welfare of Canada-we find them in the cities along the St. Lawrence and around the Great Lakes-were the men who sold the government the material that went into the Hudson Bay railway. They were quite satisfied that the project was all right so long as they were getting orders from the government; but the very day that they had sold the government the last contract, then the project was no longer feasible and the work ceased on the road. I am convinced of the truth of this.
I think the late government owes an explanation to the people of the country why work was stopped on the Hudson Bay railway in 1917. I think the western members at that time, I care not to what party they belong, whether to the Progressive party, the Liberal party or the Conservative party, all acquiesced, and therefore they all owe an explanation to the people of western Canada for allowing the work to be stopped. If one is curious enough to examine Hansard of 1921 he will find a discussion on the Hudson Bay railway, in which the government explained how lack of money and inability to obtain supplies and labour were responsible for discontinuing the work, sandwiched in between two sections of a debate on the Canadian merchant marine, on a vote of 88,000,000 for the building of vessels on which S64,000,000 had already been expended, most of it subsequent to the war. These vessels were built at a cost of $194 per ton, patently an impossible price if the ships were expected to earn dividends; and the defence of the expenditure, which was boldly made on the floor of the House, was that this outlay was necessary to cope with unemployment in and about Montreal. The government's remedy of strict economy was apparently designed purely for local application; and certainly the west got a good stiff dose of it.
I wonder sometimes if eastern members and easterners generally appreciate the extent to which the solvency of western Canada is dependent to-day upon the completion of the Husdon Bay railway. One of the largest business men in the city of Winnipeg, a man who has been in business in Winnipeg for thirty years and who is rated in Bradstreets at over $3,000,000, said to me only a short time ago, "Ward, in my business it is no longer a question of prosperity or of making dividends; it is a question of its solvency. And unless you complete the Hudson Bay
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward

railway within a very reasonable time I fear the effect of present conditions on my business.', I believe that can truthfully be said of two-thirds of the business men of western Canada.
Now, all we ask is a fair show; we are not [DOT]asking for any special privilege. I have here a statement which I have prepared and which I think probably will be of interest to the House as well as to eastern Canada. In it I have attempted to show that not one dollar of the cost of the Hudson Bay railway has been assessed against the people of eastern Canada; nor will it be necessary to assess one dollar for its completion. I think this outstanding fact is lost sight of by the jealous champions of "economy." who are anxious to see the whole scheme relegated to the limbo of past and forgotten undertakings, that as far back as 1882 the Land Act provided that the cost of the Hudson Bay railway should be defrayed by grants of public land in the northwest, and that in 1908 when the government had decided to build the railway to the bay the Dominion Lands Act was amended by Hon. Mr. Oliver, with the consent of parliament, to provide that the cost of the undertaking should be met by proceeds from the sale of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads in certain western areas particularly interested in the completion of the route. And while it is true that the amendments to the act did not specifically provide the earmarkings of the fund for this purpose, yet Mr. Oliver made it plain that the object was to create a new source of revenue which would not add anything to the eastern burden of taxation, nor constitute any additional drain on the treasury. Mr. Oliver, speaking in the House of Commons on June 23, 1908, said, as reported in Hansard at page 11,152:
There is I believe sufficient to achieve the purpose we have in view and not sufficient to warrant the anticipation of injury which seemed to lie heavy on the minds of some of our friends this time last year. At the same time we propose to relieve the mortgage, so to speak, which to-day lies against the 6.500,000 acres of land of the northwest in respect of the Hudson Bay railway. As long as that provision remains in the statute books, it is a notice by parliament to the world that, in the estimation of parliament, it is a proper policy to grant 6,500,000 acres of land in order to construct a railway from the Saskatchewan to the Hudson bay. That is not in accord with the policy of this government nor is it in accord with its administration, but by passing this bill, we relieve ourselves of any claims, past or present or future, against that 6,500,000 acres. The difference between the proposal in this bill and the provision in the Lands Act is this:
That if the provisions of the Lands Act regarding a grant to the Hudson Bay railway were implemented under the practice that formerly prevailed, whatever company should build that road would have the right to select 6,500,000 acres wherever they might see fit throughout the Northwest Territories and upon the 
completion of the road this land would become their absolute property, to be held by them until they could secure such prices as they might see fit to exact.
It was under this policy that 32.000,000 acres which have been alienated were held and a large part of it is being held to-day, a burden which has to be carried by the settlers of the west-
I hope the House will notice this:
-who will ultimately have to buy the land and dig the price out of it by their toil, enterprise and saving. Instead of taking that course we propose to allow the purchase by actual settlers, on settlement conditions of, say, 5,000,000 acres of land, realizing thereby out of a fixed and moderate price per acre sufficient money to meet the requirements of the government in respect of the Hudson Bay railway. Under the system that prevails of land grants to railways which we are displacing by this bill, the enhancement in values by reason of the settlement and improvement of the country enures to the benefit of the settlers. This is radically different to the Lands Act as it stands. There is no money which a settler who builds up a home on the prairie can make out of his land which he does not earn, and who, I ask, is better entitled to the enhanced value of the land by reason of settlement than the man whose settlement gave enhanced value? It is because the settler will have the benefit of the enhancement in value of the land that I ask the approval of the House to this bill.
The House did approve the bill, Mr. R. L. Borden, then leader of the opposition, however, remarking:
And, if not an acre of land is sold in ten years, I trust, and am led to believe, the Hudson Bay railway project will still go on in the meantime and without delay.
It is to be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal of Mr. Oliver made it necessary for actual homesteaders or bona fide settlers to provide the revenue required for the project. Homesteaders in the area through which the railway would run could pre-empt an extra 160 acres of land for S3 an acre; in other words, those who contributed to the fund were those most directly interested in the Hudson Bay railway enterprise. Mr. Oliver estimated the cost of the 500 miles of road at, roughly, $15,000,000, and in this he made a wonderfully accurate calculation, for we find on examination of the records that a little over $14,000,000 has already been expended, and according to the evidence given by Deputy Minister Bell-and I hope the House will get this very clearly-in 1919 $1,000,000 would have completed the road. I think it is an awful indictment, an indictment that will stand against the government of that day for all time to come, that they did not go ahead at that time and complete the road. It will be seen that the proceeds from the sale of these lands amounted to about $28,000,000, or sufficient, even at this date, to complete the road and put the whole enterprise in first class shape, and in addition provide for thp construction of some grain elevators.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward
I am tempted at this point, Mr. Speaker, to remind the House how much more carefui and accurate was Mr. Oliver in his estimate than were some of his predecessors. In 1895, and again in the general election of 1896, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues stumped Ontario in the interests of the National Transcontinental railway, informing the people that that enterprise would cost not more than $13,000,000. Years later, when the people of Canada were compelled to take over this same railway, which in the meantime had passed from political propaganda into an actual railway, it cost them the great sum of $357,000,000.
Under the act of 1908 the following sales of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads were made-and here is proof of what we have ahvays contended, that there has never been any assessment whatever upon eastern Canada for the construction of this railway: Saskatchewan:	Acres	Acres
Pre-emptions.. .. 4,371,200 Homesteads.. .. 776,320 Alberta :
Pre-emptions.. .. 2,573,600 Homesteads.. .. 329,600
In other words, a total of 8,050,720 acres of land was dealt with. It would be found by anyone who cares to look up the records that a great deal more land than the actual amount set apart by Mr. Oliver was sold. He valued the pre-empted lands at $15,290,059, and the homestead lands at $3,269,102; but as a matter of fact, as I say, they sold a great deal more than that. On the basis of Mr. Oliver's estimate the pre-emptions alone would have amounted to $20,834,000, or a little more than has been expended on the railway and harbour up to date.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Now, Sir, the hon. member
for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) referred to the possibilities of the two ports. I think I told the House last session that I had visited Port Nelson myself, and while perfectly ignorant of what is required to constitute a harbour, yet I do claim to have some horse sense.
On that occasion we could see no particular obstacle in the way of making Port Nelson a safe harbour. In my own constituency there is a little lake twenty to twenty-five miles long by ten miles wide, and almost every day in the summer you will observe a much heavier sea there than any that prevailed in the harbour during the week we were at Port Nelson. I would say that at no time would a large canoe not have been quite safe in the harbour during that period, and that it was probably the most dangerous of the year, from the 17th to the 23rd of September.
A criticism that has recently been directed against the Hudson Bay project is that the grain movement of western Canada would not coincide with the period of safe navigation of the Hudson strait. That probably is to a certain degree true, but not any more so than it is true in respect to the period of navigation of the Great Lakes. For example, there were only 48,000,000 buhels of grain shipped from the head of the lakes last year before the close of navigation. I would say that, roughly speaking, the export of grain from western Canada that will have to pass through the ports of Fort William and Port Arthur will probably be 200,000,000 or 250,000,000 bushels. So it will be seen that as it is, only a very small percentage of the grain passes out through those ports before navigation closes. It has been estimated by shipping experts that if a farmer living in the district of Saskatoon were to bill two cars of grain, on the same date to Liverpool, one via Hudson bay and the other via Montreal, the car billed via Port Nelson might very well be in Europe- in Liverpool, if you like-ground into flour and baked into bread before the other car had reached Montreal. It takes an average of one month between the time a car of grain is billed at the local elevator and the time it is discharged from an elevator in Montreal to an ocean-going liner, and it is estimated that grain can be delivered in any port in Europe via Hudson bay in less than a month from the time it is shipped out. It would be of infinite value to western Canada if we could deliver our grain on the European market two weeks earlier than we are doing at present. I have been told by some of the older millers of Canada that the mills all over the world are short of Canadian hard wheat from April right through until our hard wheat starts moving to the market. The reason why there is a premium on Canadian hard wheat at that period of the year, is because of the competition for the securing of that hard wheat. to mix with the softer wheats
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward

that are obtained from the more southern countries during the winter months. So that if the Hudson bay route will give us an advantage of two weeks; if we can deliver our grain in the markets of the world two weeks earlier via that route than we can via Montreal, that is a benefit which would be incalculable.
My own impression after having visited the bay is that the opinion held by many men that the route would not be safe for navigation for more than three months in the year is entirely preposterous. I was at Port Nelson about the 20th of September. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) has told the House what the weather was like when he was there. I do not remember what he said the date was, but when I was there the weather was just as warm, I am sure, as it would be on the Niagara peninsula at that time of the year. During our entire trip, which extended into October, I kept a record of the mean temperature, and when I got back home and summed it all up I was amazed to find that it averaged, day and night, 55 degrees faren-heit. I venture to say that it is doubtful whether in any other part of Canada the temperature at that time of the year would be as high as it was on the shore of Hudson bay. I cannot believe for a minute that with the weather such as it was at Port Nelson, there would be huge ice floes and so on 400 miles up the bay, or at Hudson straits, and that the whole thing might be frozen up. Nor do I think that the Almighty placed a great inland sea in the heart of the American continent without a purpose, and I believe that purpose was to serve the great western country.
Only a few days ago I had an interview with the chief of the Geological Survey here in Ottawa and I asked him what he knew about the iron ore of the Belcher islands. The Survey branch have sent men to those islands to study the quantity, quality and
5 p.m. value of that iron ore, and he tells me that it is by all odds the most extensive and valuable deposit in Canada. The ore averages about 45 per cent high grade iron, which is as high as anything else we have in Canada. In extent we have nothing else to compare with it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could go on for another hour in dealing with this matter, but surely enough has been said. We have shown that the Hudson Bay railway has not cost eastern Canada one red cent. It is purely a western project, But while it is a western project, I claim that it is also a national project. We have frequently been asked why western Can-
ada did not build the Hudson Bay railway itself and not be calling upon the federal parliament to deal with the matter. Well, in reply to that I would say that when the west is given a reasonable deal in connection with the control of her natural resources; when British Columbia assumes the responsibility of the development and maintenance of Vancouver harbour; when Prince Rupert harbour and dry docks are maintained by the province of British Columbia, and when Ontario does likewise for the port of Toronto and also takes over all liabilities in connection with the Welland canal and the Trent canal; when the province of Quebec charges itself with the task of maintaining and developing the St. Lawrence route, the port of Montreal, and a score of other national undertakings in that province; when it is agreed that the Canadian cost of developing the St. Lawrence waterways from Montreal to Toronto is to be met by the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; when these things are done it will be high time for eastern Canada to expect the west to develop that great national undertaking, the Hudson bay route. But I venture to say that none of these things will be done. The west is paying more than her fair share of the development of these enterprises, and for that reason the east is not likely to adopt any other policy than the present one.
I have mentioned in this connection the Welland ship canal, and I wish to make just a reference to that undertaking. I stated a year ago, Mr. Speaker, and I want to repeat it now. that neither the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) nor anyone else in Canada can prove-and I challenge them to do so-that the Welland ship canal is worth fifteen cents to the public of this country. The Welland ship canal will never reduce the carrying charges of grain by one-thirtieth of one per cent,-and I want this to be on record. Nor will it ever reduce the carrying charges of goods into western Canada, The Welland ship canal will benefit no one except the lake carrying companies, and probably the cities of Toronto, Port Arthur and Fort William Immediately the Welland ship canal is completed, if it is of any value, what will we find? We will have the Port Colbome elevators scrapped; they will become a pile of concrete. We will have the members from Toronto down here demanding another $20,000,000 for the building of grain elevators at Toronto, and we will go on paying exactly the same that we are paying to-day in carrying charges.
I was astonished when I saw in the estimates this year another $15,000,000 for what to me

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward
is a most unjustifiable expenditure. The only other expenditure made during the last thirty years in Canada that compares with it at all, to my mind, is the expenditure on the government merchant marine. The minister might very well have foregone the expenditure on the Welland ship canal for this year and spent a little of this money on the Hudson Bay railway. Of course, that may be his intention in any case.
The government is being urged to inaugurate an aggressive immigration policy. With this I am largely in agreement, as I believe the future of this country depends in a very large degree upon our ability to attract, retain and maintain settlers in this country. But that can only be done, Sir, by the adoption of policies that will make it reasonably possible for people to succeed when they come here. The one great stride that could be made in that direction would be to complete the Hudson bay route at once and thus with one stroke reduce the cost of living in the three prairie provinces by anywhere from $100,000,000 to $200,000,000. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) smiles. I may tell him that I delivered an address at a certain town in Saskatchewan a year ago during the course of which I made that same statement. Shortly afterwards I received a letter from the Toronto Saturday Night stating that a reporter who had been at the meeting had reported me as having made that statement, and it appeared to them so preposterous that the editor hesitated to publish it without first sommunicating with me.
I took the Canada Year Book, and in reply gave figures absolutely proving my statement. 1 worked out a rather comprehensive statement showing that $175,000,000 per year is being lost through the non-completion of the road and sent it to the Toronto Saturday Night and requested them to publish it but, of course, needless to say, they never did publish it. It can be proven absolutely that western Canada has been losing for many years a sum ranging anywhere from one hundred to two hundred millions of dollars through the non-completion of the Hudson Bay railway. Take the grain trade alone, and it costs western Canada on the average $82,000,000 per year-or has done since 1920-to transport our grain crop from the head of the lakes to tide water, to say nothing about all the other exports and imports from or into western Canada. And it must also be remembered that the head of the lakes is one hundred and thirty miles farther from the average railway station in western Canada than is Port Nelson. So
upon the basis of the present railway freight rates you could add another $15,000,000 to the figures mentioned, which brings the cost of transporting our grain from the head of the lakes to tide water, to practically $100,000,000. That charge would undoubtedly be saved if the grain was carried out via Hudson bay. I do not contend for one minute, I am not sc foolish as to entertain the view, that we could in one year, or ten years, or probably in twenty years, develop the Hudson bay route to the extent that would enable this large percentage of our grain to be carried out by the Hudson bay route. But that route would certainly be a leveller in the matter of rates and it would remove the need for some magna charta such as the Crowsnest pass rates in the west. Western Canada can never relinquish its claim and its hold upon the Crowsnest rates, it matters not what the consequences may be without some proper equivalent. Out there we are marooned in the heart of a great continent, fifteen hundred to two thousand miles from tide water. We have not the advantages of water competition such as you have in eastern Canada, and there is no limit to which western Canada will not go to retain the Crowsnest pass rates -at least until we get the Hudson bay route in operation and it has proven a success. The opening of this great national route to the north would bring the average settler of western Canada anywhere from one thousand to twelve hundred miles closer to the markets of the world; and it would remedy the situation which the government is now facing of establishing a new -freight rate structure such as will be acceptable to western Canada and all parts of the country.
We hear a great deal about the feasibility of the route, and in that connection some very extravagant statements have been made. I think the Minister of Railways himself made the statement last year that it would cost approximately $20,000,000 to complete the road. I am very largely in agreement with the views of the late W. A. Bowden, chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, who, when giving evidence before the Senate committee, said:
The feasibility of the route might well be determined by the operation for a few years of vessels by the government. I think twelve vessels; six to be owned by the government which might have 50 per cent extra for ice strengthening, and six ordinary tramp steamers would be chartered. This would be the basis on the experiment.
In my opinion that would be a very excellent experiment to make. I would be entirely opposed however, to any huge ex-
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Ward
