speechtext: If the government does not undertake the development of the ports of the country how would those ports be developed to the extent necessary to take care of the shipment of grain or cattle from western Canada, or the rest of the import or export trade? If the government did not provide for this expenditure who would undertake the work?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I am not complaining of the development of the ports in question. But what I do say is that these works are not so necessary or so pressing as the Hudson Bay railway which stands in a class by itself. As to the need of the latter enterprise I can take my hon. friend to my own district where eighty-six families left one section,. a section of about eight miles square, last year owing to the lack of needed transportation facilities. We hear hon. gentlemen to my right talking about the troubles that our Canadian manufacturers are having, and how they are becoming insolvent and that sort of thing. They do not know what they are talking about. Premier Bracken made the statement a little less than a year ago that he believed 90 per cent of the farmers of Manitoba were hopelessly insolvent, and I do not think he is far out. When you consider that it costs an average of 63 per cent of the value of production in western Canada to ship to tidewater, you will understand why they are insolvent. That is what is the matter with the manufacturing and the mercantile business at the present time. The farmer has no purchasing power. He cannot pay out 63 per cent of the value of this product and have any money left to purchase material.
I would like to make a final reference to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and to that famous speech on the budget that he delivered the other day. I would call it a herring speech. I visited the market the next day after be had spoken, I wanted to

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Lovie
buy some fish. I went to a fish vendor and he had nothing but suckers, and he wanted- fifteen -cents a pound for them. I complained about the price, and he said, "Yes, it is high, but (the Minister of Agriculture -has cornered ail the red herring and it affects the price all along the line". I am not in agreement with some hon. members who have spoken before me in congratulating the minister on his conversion to the Hudson Bay project. I am quite sure that if the electors of the constituency of Regina had known that the minister was not a convert to the Hudson Bay railway and to the port of Nelson proposition he would not be occupying a seat in this House to-day, and I venture to say that unless he is a convert to the Hudson bay route and the port of Nelson he will not occupy a seat in the next parliament. I am not given to prophesying, but I think that is a prophecy very easily made. I hope we will not go away from this parliament disappointed this year. In -common with the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), I -have a very great regard for the .Minister of Railways (Mr. -Gralham), and I believe hie .is absolutely sincere when he tells us that he is desirous of seeing the road completed. I believe he would like to seie it completed- and I Ithi-nk he would like to drive the last spike in the road himself, and would like to drive it this year. If he has the interests of confederation at heart,, and if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has the interests of confederation at heart and wishes to see it continued, I would suggest to him (that he also be a convert to the immediate completion of the road. I hope that we will have the pleasure of seeing a very substantial estimate in the su-pp-lementaries for the Hudson Bay railway this year.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
In the
second week of January, 1925, at the annual banquet of the Shorthorn Breeders' Convention in the city of Brandon, in the after-dinner speeches, the ball was set rolling by Dean McKillican of the Manitoba Agricultural College, and the line of the shorthorn dairy cattle breeding was taken up, and following that line there was a discussion as to the export of cattle to the British market. Naturally the question came up as to how the expensive rail haul between the prairie provinces and Montreal could be eliminated, and along with that the depreciation in weight of live stock when carried on the railways, which was very great. No one seemed to be able to answer the question until it came to my turn, and I was pretty nearly the last speaker. Present at the meeting were Mr. Atcheson, representing the Canadian Pacific Railway, and Mr. Watson representing -the Canadian National, and when I mentioned the feasibility of the Hudson Bay railway as a means of transporting cattle to the ocean ports with about five or six hundred miles of rail haul, the gentlemen from the railways deprecated the proposition, threw cold water on it, and said that the Hudson bay was ice-bound and consequently would not be feasible for such a purpose. But the men who were raising the cattle-and there was a large number of them at the banquet-immediately started to cheer; that is what they had been waiting for, and that is what they are waiting for to-day. If the stock raising interests of western Canada are ever going to amount to anything some means must be found of eliminating the long rail haul between the stockyards in St. Boniface and tidewater, and the shortest route for the transportation of cattle is by a railway to Hudson bay. It is a well known fact that cattle lose weight rapidly when carried on the railways, but when they are transported in vessels on the ocean they are just as apt to gain weight as to lose it. They will certainly hold their own. We want to develop the British market, just as we want to develop all available markets, so that Great Britain will take an unlimited quantity of high class cattle. They do not want anything else but high class cattle, and Canadians have not yet been educated along the line of raising a class of cattle fit for export. The American market will take all the cattle of inferior grades at a price. If we raised high class cattle we would certainly be able to find a market for them.
In reference to the statement that Hudson bay is ice-bound, I might say after listening to the debates tvhich have been held in this House, I am convinced that such is not the case. I quote now from Hansard of June 29, 1923, and I find the following opinion expressed :
As far as I can see it with the icebound bay-
That is in reference to Hudson bay. And now in contradiction of that let me quote here, a speech by John A. Campbell, Commissioner of Northern Manitoba, a man who has travelled all over the country and who knows. He says:
Hudson Bay
This is a vast inland sea; a body of salt water eight hundred miles long by five hundred miles wide. It does not freeze over.
I have here, reproduced from the Manitoba Free Press of June 14, 1924, -a photograph taken of Port Nelson on January 24, 1919-midwinter. It shows open water in the bay on that date. So that must certainly dispel the idea that Hudson bay is a frozen body

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Lovie

of water. It is a vast inland sea eight hundred miles long and five hundred miles wide.
Mr. Campbell stated further:
The water is deep, and there are no obstructing rocks or islands and practically no icebergs to interfere with navigation. There are no special obstacles to be overcome by navigators, and all reports go to show that this immense body of water can be as readily and easily navigated as almost any other.
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) in his address this afternoon, mentioned the fact that people were apt to form erroneous opinions of western Canada, and that brought to my mind an incident that happened to myself personally about twenty-two years ago on board ship on the Atlantic when I was accosted by a gentleman whose home was in the city of Milwaukee. He said, "I hear you come from Manitoba?" I said "Yes." He said, "I would like to find out what the country is like. I have some friends who are talking of going to that country. Is it possible for a woman to live there and js the climate such that people can live there during the winter?" I said: "I have been twenty years in Manitoba and I have a wife and my two eldest youngsters with me. I will let you see them so that you can see whether they can live through the winter." He confessed that he was very much surprised. He had heard that the country was not fit for white people to live in. Some people have the same idea regarding the Hudson bay country. When the Hudson Bay railway is completed to tidewater, the hardy British sailors are going to bring their steamers in there and take out cargoes of grain. They are going to prove that that port was placed by the Almighty in the heart of the American continent, not for nothing, but to be the gateway of the great granary of the empire, and also for the grain of North and South Dakota and probably the eastern half of Montana. That is the nearest point to seaboard they can have.
As regards shipping wheat from there, we must always remember that there is no part of the country where wheat is grown as a commercial proposition that is further from the seaboard than the prairie provinces are from the Atlantic seaboard. That makes it harder for the people of the prairie provinces to produce wheat at a profit. We are looking forward to the utilization of the port of Nelson as the means of having our grain reach the seaboard with as short a rail haul as possible.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth time that I have risen in this House to speak on this subject, and I do not propose at this time
[.Mr. Lovie.]
to repeat the arguments that I have presented in the sessions immediately preceding. I along with my colleagues here have attempted to place before the members of this House almost innumerable arguments why this project should be taken lip and proceeded with in its proper order. I recall that I have myself attempted to point out the advantages of this road and particularly its directness to the European market. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Lovie) has just pointed out its advantage to the stock raiser and grain grower. Last year, I think it was, I placed on Hansard certain figures which, on later consideration, I found to be very conservative as to the quantity of grain that was immediately tributary to the line leading in the direction of and almost to Hudson 'bay. I have also placed on Hansard reports of various men whose opinions are worth while and deserving of consideration as to the feasibility of this route. I do not think there are many arguments that have not been canvassed and presented.
I want, however, at this time to call the attention of the House again to the very moderate language of the resolution which we are debating this afternoon. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) is asking the House simply to reaffirm a decision which it made some two years ago when it was decided that the Hudson Bay railway should be proceeded with in the proper sequence of public works that are under way. All that we are asking, at the present time is that the House should decide that this work of great national importance should be proceeded with in its proper sequence. I agree heartily with the statement made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) as to what would be proper and acceptable in the way of furthering this scheme. The people of western Canada are demanding in no uncertain tones, that it must be proceeded with, but it is unnecessary, I think, for me to say that the people of western Canada are not unreasonable, that they realize that neither this government nor any other government can or should expend huge amounts of public money at one time, and that time the present. But they demand that this work slhall be continued, and that a reasonable share-may I so put it-of the money that is expended on public works should be expended on that project which is dear to them and which is apparently, in their estimation, going to be of great value to them. If the laying of the steel on the grade that is already there were continued, no complaint, no grumbling would come from the people of western Can-

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Stewart (Humboldt)
ada as to a lack of money being spent on the port.
The development of our ports, as has already been pointed out, is an expensive matter, and a matter that, not only because of the expense but because of the use of our ports, is pre-eminently a national affair. It is not something that can be done in a day. It is very easy for us. viewing the ports of our country and the state of comparative completeness to which some of them have attained, to say that they are entirely satisfactory, and then, pointing to a port such as Nelson which, in the barrenness and openness of the very beginning of the work, there, does not compare very favourably with a port such as Montreal, or Halifax or Vancouver, to say that it is altogether impossible that the port of Nelson should ever compare with those ports. But any person who would make such a statement is not giving due consideration to the history of the ports of this country.
I want for a few moments this afternoon to direct the attention of the House to the development of one of our great water routes which has at least two very important ports upon it. That is the St. Lawrence route with the ports of Quebec and Montreal served by it. I do not want anything that I may say to be taken as casting any reflection upon the wisdom of the expenditure, nor to make any statement as to the amount that was spent having been too great. I point out simply that it cost many millions of dollars and it took may years to develop that route to the comparatively perfect stage in which we find it to-day. That route was used, I suppose, nearly three hundred years ago as a route for commerce, and because for the life-time of this generation it has been looked upon as a safe route, we have, I think, as Canadians, almost forgotten that at one time the St. Lawrence river route was not considered a safe highway for the larger boats of commerce and that it was never expected it would develop into a highway for the trading vessels of the world. For two hundred years that route was used by the smaller vessels and used even by them with great danger and loss. During those very same years the Hudson Bay route was in use with less loss than the St. Lawrence route. At the time of confederation no great sums of money had been expended in developing the St. Lawrence waterway up to the port of Montreal. It was considered a highly perilous highway for large vessels to take, and reports that were made to parliament shortly after confederation bore out that statement. I have a few notes as to some of the figures that were given.
178i
The report I have in my hand is one made to the Minister of Navigation in the year 1867 by the Quebec Board of Trade, and I want to quote just a few words from that report:
The most urgent and important requirement is the removal of the lighthouse (with its miserable light) from the centre of Red island, and the substitution of a Lightship at the east end of the Red islaad reef, with a steam whistle for thick weather. The report upon the wreck of the Ellen in 1866 (when the whole crew perished) will show that at present the reef extends fully two and one-half miles southeast of the lighthouse and that in foggy weather a ship is ashore before the island light can be seen. During the present season-
That is 1867.
-no less than five ships have struck upon this island.
The report goes on to demand another lightship, declaring that there was sufficient proof of the necessity for it. This proof, it says, is to be found in the fact that in 1864 four vessels were lost at that particular point. In the year 1869 a total of 600 vessels used tihe ports of Quebec and Montreal and of these twenty-six were wrecked either on the inward voyage or on the outward course. Compare that with the figures in relation to Hudson bay. The Hudson's Bay Company made use of the bay as well as of Port Nelson for a matter of some two hundred years, and in that two hundred years, with 750 sailings, only two vessels were lost. A judicious ejqjenditure of money over a considerable number of years has brought tihe St. Lawrence route up to a state of development in which, we no longer consider it dangerous. As a matter of fact, I do not recall having heard of a vessel being wrecked on that route, in quite a number of years, from any other cause than collision. All the dangers have been removed and the route has been developed to a state of perfection by the expenditure of very considerable sums of money which, if they were totalled up to tihe present time, including the cost of maintenance from year to year, would be far in excess of $100,000,000. The capital expenditure alone is now something over $90,000,000 over that 200 miles. Perhaps hon. gentlemen may think this comparison has little to do with the route into Port Nelson, but I hold that it has. It has been by means of modern navigation aids that the St. Lawrence has been made a safe highway for the largest vessels that travel the Atlantic ocean, and the same aid applied to Hudson bay would place it in a fairly favourable position to compete with the S't. Lawrence route.
It has been brought to our attention at various times, and recently by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), that there

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Stewart (Humboldt)
are certain mud flats at the mouth of the Nelson river and that it will probably be a quite expensive matter to make a thoroughly satisfactory channel through those mud flats to the open bay. But I think that if we accept that statement seriously we are overlooking the fact that there is through these mud flats at the present time a channel which gives a sufficient draught of water for ordinarysized vessels; in fact, it gives the same draught of water to-day as there was on the St. Lawrence for fifteen years after confederation.

About seventeen feet; no, an hon. member corrects me and says it is nineteen. And I believe that is correct. But that of course is at low tide; the tide at that point would add another four or five feet. On the St. Lawrence route today -there is a draught of thirty feet, but we must not forget that this has been made possible by considerable dredging in lake St. Peter; and it has cost in that particular area alone, I am told, something like $15,000,000 to achieve this result. Nor was this condition brought about without many disappointments; it was only after many starts had been made and the work had been abandoned and resumed that the route as it is to-day became possible. Now there is a highway through the flats of that lake 450 feet in width and thirty feet deep, all the result of work done during the last fifty years.
If, as has been suggested this afternoon, the present government would undertake to lay the steel on the graded roadway to the port of Nelson and make even sufficient provision there for tramp steamers to find their way in, I for one, having advocated1 or pleaded, if you like, for the completion of the route, would consider that a satisfactory step to begin with, and I should be willing to leave it to possible developments, in the way of navigation and in the traffic that would be available, to prove whether the port were worthy of further consideration and whether, in the case of that port as with otheT ports that we have developed, we should continue steadily to expend money to improve it and make it safer and more convenient than it is at the present time.
I contend that we need to-day men who have something of a forward vision. Too many of us are looking back over the past; we see what has been accomplished and when we contemplate the things that lie ahead of us awaiting development we are fearful. Had

the men who undertook to develop the port of Montreal or the port of Quebec, or foT that matter any great port in Canada, looked at the matter with the fear and trembling which some hon. gentlemen profess to have in regard to the port of Nelson, we should have had no Maritime connections at the present time; we should have been isolated. We want forward-looking statesmen who are willing to take a chance on the future just as our forefathers took chances on a country which *was held up to them as rocky and ice-bound but which they made productive, a country which is now clamouring for greater outlets than it has.

I

Now, what businesses will be helped by the completion and operation of the Hudson Bay railway? The grain business will not be helped. You will not have any ships sailing out of Hudson bay ports after the middle of October. How much of your grain are you going to get down to Hudson bay ports before the middle of October? But is it wise to spend more money upon a project with the tremendous and certain disadvantages of the Hudson bay route, when the great outlet of the grain from the westward plains is not eastward but westward? What you need is better railway accommodation to bring a lot of your grain to the Pacific ports and not to Atlantic ports at all. That is what you really need.
Now, there is the question of this port, Port Nelson. What I am told is this: The Nelson river is a tremendous river; it runs through a lot of arable land and brings down every year an immense amount of silt. Although it is quite true that the current scours a certain channel at Port Nelson, that channel is more or less a narrow one and if you are going to have a large port there you will have to spend millions upon millions of dollars on it and you will have to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars year by year to keep it dredged out. I was told while. I was in the west the winter before last that the proper port was Fort Churchill. I was told that at Fort Churchill there was a good natural harbour and that it was not exposed to the disadvantage of being filled up with silt.
Now, this project may come in due time, Mr. Speaker, but I would ask you, .'and through you the members of the House, not to regard this matter as a matter of faith and doctrine. It should not be regarded in that fashion. It is true governments may have committed themselves to it. It is true a certain contract may have been entered into. If it is thought wise to carry out that contract equitably it should be done; if not an adjustment of accounts should take place. But some of us have the idea that it is going to help us, in spite of the evidence placed

before us, we should support a proposal which those best informed regard as a very doubtful desirability, or if not doubtful desirability, certainly doubtful practicability. With the finances of the country in the shape they are in, I want to see economy all along the line. I do not ask hon. members to give up the Hudson Bay railway idea without being prepared to advocate the giving up of many propositions nearer home. My voice as long as it is to be heard in this House will be heard for economy all along the line, ancl I do not think the present project is one which will appeal to the economic sentiment and feeling which I would like to see mobilized in the entire country, a feeling in favour of eliminating every expense we can get along without.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was speaking against the resolution which is under discussion at the present time. He raised several objections to the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, one being that no ships could pass out of Port Nelson after October, and because of that it would be of no use for handling the crop of that year. I am afraid the hon. member is not very familiar with the methods used in moving the crops of western Canada or he would not have made that statement. The knowledge of all the people in eastern Canada in regard to the handling of the crop is not so limited as that of the hon. member, but I will quote in reply to his statement from a paper read by Frederick William Cowie, B.Sc., M.E.I.C., before the Montreal branch of the Engineering Institute of Canada on April 19, 1923. Dealing with this very objection which my hon. friend mentioned he said:
What about the argument that " relatively short period of safe navigation does not coincide with the period of crop movement "? The writer has seen time and time again, new crop from the Canadian west, at Montreal elevators, from August 20 to 25. This grain could be at Nelson a full week earlier.
That leaves considerable time, Mr. Speaker, to get the grain loaded and out When it can be in Nelson a week earlier than August 20 or 25. He goes on to say:
Neither the Hudson bay route nor the St. Lawrence route provides an ideal season of navigation, but there is a great similarity, the critical period of each being September, October, and part of November.
Then the hon. member raised objection to the port of Nelson, saying that on account of the silt which was carried down from the prairie country bars formed in the channel, and it was not a very good harbour for that reason-the channel, he said, was very narrow. In reply to that I want to read an extract from the evidence of Mr. McLachlan, the engineer, regarding the channel at Nelson. Engineer McLachlan in a sworn statement before the Senate committee in 1920, said:
This new channel is a natural channel without any dredging. The depth is 20 feet at low tide, 33.7 at high tide and about 40 feet at spring tide. The width of the channel at the narrowest point is 1,200 feet.
Then my hon. friend passes on to the straits. He said he could support the whole project if the straits were only navigable for any length of time during the year. Well, in connection with that we have the evidence of Mr. J. W. Tyrell who spent considerable time on the strait making observations. He says:
We had an observation point 400 feet above the sea, and I had a telescope built into a cairn on top of that cliff, and I used to go up every day to look at the conditions through the telescope. I could see a long distance, clean out to the middle of the straits. The ice was almost constantly on the move as in the tidal current, the maximum of which was eight miles an hour.
Outside of two months there were open leads all the time. They were the months of January and February, I think. My belief is that the straits are navigable for about five months in the year, figuring on aids to navigation-July, August, 'September, Octobejr, and November. I think the ice at the eastern and western extremity of the straits would not interfere particularly during those five months.
I need not go into the history of the work done in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. That has been gone over many times in this House, and I do not think it is necessary to take up more time by repeating it. From the year 1910 until 1918 work was carried on continuously on this railroad and at the harbour of Port Nelson. During that time 332 miles of road were completed and laid with eighty pound steel rails, mile long sidings were constructed at various short intervals along the way to facilitate the handling of grain, and three immense steel bridges built. I think these structures are amongst the largest of the steel bridges that have been built in western Canada. Now, the government were going on laying steel until 1918 when the work was mysteriously stopped. The general impression in western Canada is that powerful interests who feared the competition of this route brought pressure to bear upon the government, with the result that the work was stopped and the whole project abandoned. This went so far that an order was actually issued to tear up the rails. From

Hudson Bay Ry.

Mr. Bancroft
the beginning of this process right up to the present time a campaign of false and misleading statements has been carried on in many of the leading papers in eastern Canada. The only excuse that was ever offered for abandoning this work was the excuse of economy-economy in national expenditures. Having embarked upon this policy of national economy in 1918 we should have made some very substantial savings in the seven years that have passed since then. We abandoned the Hudson bay project which offered the greatest economic possibility of any of the public works under construction at that time, and we saved $2,000,000 by so doing. This policy of economy was apparently confined to the Hudson Bay railway. If you peruse the records of this House you will find that since 1918 we have spent over $97,000,000 on eight public undertakings in this country, none of which offers the economic possibilities of the Hudson bay route. During the period from and including 1918, including also the estimates before the House for 1925, the expenditures on the following eight undertakings were as follows:

speechtext:
I think the Hudson bay project would pay interest on the investment
TMr. Bancroft.!
too. I say further that if I did not tlhink so I would not be here advocating it. Now in addition to these large expenditures that are being carried on at this time, we must not forget that a great deal of money has been spent to make this St. Lawrence ship channel more navigable than it is at the present time.
I have before me an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press headed:
When millions did not count.
That- article says in part:
When the ocean greyhounds of to-day pause in their race across the Atlantic, and pick up at Father point, a pilot to steer them through the St. Lawrence to Quebec and thence to Montreal, the passengers forget the dangers which lurk beneath the blue waters in the glorious prospect of the shores.
If they stopped to consider they would realize thaf their pathway has been made safe because of scores of millions of dollars which have been expended in the erection of lighthouses, the placing of buoys, and the dredging out of dangerous reefs and shoals. Figuratively their ship is sailing smoothly on a river of gold.
Later on this article says:
The capital expenditure on this route as disclosed in the official reports of the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Ottawa, may be tabulated as follows:
Dredging	 $16,326,206
Montreal harbour	 36,330,000
Quebec harbour	 11,990,995
Aids (such as buoys and lights) 4,147,113 Radio, wireless and similar equipment	 1,000,000
Total	 $69,794,914
These figures do not include the current year when an additional $5,000,000 was voted for the Montreal harbour.
That was last year.
Neither do the figures contain the vast total of the upkeep charges which this year total more than $700,000 and last year more than $800,000. The Quebec harbour this year requires $500,000 which parliament has given. At the very least these figures would swell the total to $90,000,000.
Then the article proceeds to give some figures in regard to the route which my hon. friend from HumboMt (Mr. Stewart) referred to this afternoon, and among other things it tells how the difficulties were overcome to make it the great waterway that it is to-day. It- says:
Judicious expenditure of money, however, has brought about a vast change in the navigability of the river until to-day it is rarely the case that ships are injured from any cause other than collision.
From Quebec to Montreal by river is a little better than 180 miles, and the dogged determination shown by the federal government and the harbour commission of Montreal in carving out of the river a passage which would enable the city to become an ocean port, has never been excelled in the history of Canada. To give a detailed account of the struggle of those years would require too much space, but there were many failures, many partial successes before the final triumph. Lake St. Peter presented the greatest obstacle with its

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Bancroft
mud flats. Here the work of years was abandoned and a fresh start made, not once but several times.
In the end, however, nature yielded and to-day the great liners steam along a highway-not many times wider than Portage avenue-which has been made by man. When it is considered that there is more than 100 miles of dredged channel and that throughout ail that distance the passage must be marked out carefully and gone over each year with dredges, then the magnitude of the achievement may be realized.
I quote that to show that while there are difficulties to overcome in the Hudson bay route, we have difficulties to overcome in the St. Lawrence route and our information is that it will not take nearly as much expenditure to make the Hudson bay route feasible as has been spent on the St. Lawrence route. The people in western Canada are unanimously behind this project; but the friends of the Hudson bay route do not all live in western Canada. I have in my hand a copy of the Scientific American of June, 1923, and on the front page of that journal I find an article headed:
Hudson's Bay, the "Neglected Sea"_ by John T. Rowland.
And he tells us how he cruised the straits in a 30-foot auxiliary yawl in the summer of 1913, and he says the only difficulty he found was in taking the bearing of the ship, because the magnetic points of the compass would not work, on account of being so close to the magnetic pole, but he goes on to say that this has been overcome.
But this difficulty has since been almost magically removed by the .perfection of the gyro-compass. A ship equipped with one of these can dispense with the old-fashioned magnetic instrument entirely and steer across Hudson's bay as readily as across the Atlantic ocean.
In addition to this we have a gentleman in Montreal who is very much in favour of the route, and I am sure hon. members will be surprised to hear that. I refer to Mr. F. W. Cowie, who is engineer of the Montreal Harbour Commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
That is the gentleman who
laid out the Halifax terminals.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
He picked out a good
harbour, then.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Yes, he did that all right,
but he made a mess of it.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: It was a good harbour before he started.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
He says in this paper
read before the Montreal Institute of Engineers :
The writer dares greatly in "risking a fall " with the editor-in-chief of the Gazette, of Montreal, who so fittingly voices, and even leads commercial opinion in the east.
After no superficial study, however, the writer dares the statement, that the Hudson's bay route offers much more than "a gambler's chance of success". He has personally experienced every phase in connection with St. Lawrence river navigation, its failures and its successes.
The late Sir John Kennedy, past president of this institute, in no casual school, taught the writer that while one cannot force the mighty St. Lawrence one may make terms with it. And where in the world such prodigious difficulties, where such successes, as in the making of the artificial harbour at Montreal ?
There is only one St. Lawrence, and Canada may thank God for it. It can have no enduring rival, but is it wise and sufficient that it be relied upon alone? Those who know, will accept, that no one may be more, or even equally loyal to the St. Lawrence route, than the writer, who has given his best towards its success, in the last thirty-seven continuous years, and based on mature experience, he is of the opinion that the Hudson's bay route, under accepted limitations, offers a prize, in favour of production, worthy of fuller investigation and a better attempt to demonstrate it.
Further on in his paper he says:
The Hudson's bay route is now over three hundred years old and for over two hundred and fifty years a company of hard-headed merchants, operating for gain, with distinct success; year after year, sent one or more ships to Hudson's bay, and the records of loss are very few.
Then later on he dealt with its relation to the time problem, which I read a few minutes ago, showing that the period during which Hudson bay is open and the straits are known to be navigable is a period that fits in very nicely with the crop movement of western Canada.
The people of western Canada are practically a unit in their demands that this railway be completed. It is not only the hon. memibers who have the honour of representing western Canada in this House who are demanding it, but I think all three provincial legislatures have passed unanimous resolutions, supported by all parties, demanding the completion of this road. In addition to this the farmers' organizations of the three provinces have endorsed the project and want to see it completed immediately. Furthermore, I think every board of trade in the three prairie provinces has passed resolutions to the same effect. I have no doubt the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways and Canals have had many resolutions sent to them along this line. These people have some excuse for sending these resolutions to the government because, just prior to the election of 1921, the people of that district made it their business to find out where the leaders of the different parties stood in the matter. The secretary of the Pas Board of
2802	COMMONS
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Bancroft
Trade wrote to the Prime Minister and he replied in December, 1920, as follows:
With respect to the particular project of the Hudson Bay railway, such expression as there has been on behalf of the party was given in parliament at the time the project was inaugurated.
I would interpret that to mean that because the Liberal party had started this project in 1910, they were going to go through with what they started.
In November, 1921, they wrote to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and this was his reply regarding the completion of the Hudson Bay railway:
I have several times stated the policy of the government towards the Hudson Bay railway. I regard its completion as essential, and not only that but am most anxious that the least possible delay be allowed before its completion is finally undertaken.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) was at that time leading the party to which I belong. They wrote to him also, and these were his views on the matter:
Expressing imy own personal view, I have no hesitation in stating this road should be completed to the bay at the earliest possible moment, and I hold the further belief that eventually it will become one of <the great trade routes of the world.
In view of the unanimous demand from western Canada for the completion of this road, in view of the vast expenditures that have been carried on in other parts of the country since this project has been abandoned, and in view of the fact that the Prime Minister practically pledged himself to it before the last election and that the Minister of Railways and Canals turned the first sod and has been a strong supporter of the project, we should have this resolution accepted tonight and the work gone on with as speedily as possible.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure my hon. friends from western Canada that I have not the slightest antipathy or ill will towards that part of the country or to the hon. gentlemen who come from there. If there is anything practicable that this country can do that will benefit the western provinces, they are entitled to consideration along that line. They have their difficulties, many of them. We have our difficulties also, and we can sympathize with them. If I thought this project was feasible or practicable, I certainly would be pleased to support it. But viewing it as I do and considering it to be, commercially speaking, impracticable, having regard to my duty as a member of this House, I shall have to vote against it. I will give my reasons for doing so. Captain Read's name was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for

Brome (Mr. McMaster), and I do not know that I would have mentioned his name if it were not for that fact. Captain Read is, I think, the most experienced man in ice navigation in the Dominion of Canada at the present time. He has certainly no ill will towards the western provinces. He is not influenced by any unworthy considerations whatever. He has been in Hudson bay and Hudson strait for two years and, I think, three, placing aids to navigation in those waters. He was a ship owner and he is a master mariner. He sailed the seas with his father who was also a ship owner and a master mariner.' During the war he took at least two ice-breaking ships through the White sea to Archangel and delivered them faithfully. He has been for years operating an ice-breaking steamer in the strait of Northumberland. He knows all about winter navigation in the strait of Northumberland and the gulf of St. Lawrence. Therefore, I think his views are entitled to some consideration and he has given his views, stating his reasons for them. In the ship's log he gives the dates and actual conditions that he found in those waters during the time he was there, and anybody reading those records will come to the conclusion that the proposition is an impracticable one.
I listened this afternoon to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), who always makes a nice address and is careful of his words. He is a responsible man; anything he says is worthy of consideration; but while commending this project, he actually condemned it. I think he said there were two vessels, there were some vessels at all events, that had been beached some years ago in or near the harbour at Port Nelson and that they were still intact. They had not been broken up by the action of the sea, the waves and the wind. Why? He gave the answer himself, that the sea broke some fifteen or twenty miles-he did not say this-oS the mouth of the Nelson river. The force of the waves was broken on the sand bars before they could reach the harbour at the mouth of the river. Any man who knows anything about navigation will say that that condemns Port Nelson as a harbour.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
read engineer McLachlan's report given before the committee stating that there was a permanent channel there in which sand bars never formed?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I will come to that. There is nothing that a master mariner or mariner so much dreads as approaching a low coast where sand bars reach a considerable distance out into the sea.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hughes

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: They get into St. John harbour pretty well.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
mistaken. It is the tide he is speaking about and that is quite a different thing.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It is a tidal harbour
and there are mud flats.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It is a tidal harbour, but
there are no sand bars there. I will tell my hon. friend where there is a sand bar. There is a sand bar about three-quarters of a mile wide at the mouth of the Mersey river leading to Liverpool. I have the distance in yards and I think it is about 1,200 yards. I have this from men who have sailed in and out of Liverpool for years, and it can be verified. They say that it requires three of the most powerful sand-suction dredges in the British Empire to keep that channel open, and they are working twenty-four hours a day, 365 days in the year.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that they made a mistake in developing that port?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: My gracious, what a foolish question! If the hon. member will have patience I am sure he will see the point of my argument. There are other dredges kept in reserve which can be brought into service if one of these regular dredges becomes disabled or is being repaired. The immense shipping on that river passing in and out of Liverpool, and the tremendous tonnage involved, is justification for this enormous expenditure. Now, the sand formation at the mouth of the Nelson river, between the river and the sea, is very similar to the formation at the mouth of the Mersey.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Is this crossing the
channel or outside the channel?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Wait a moment and you will see. The channel shifts.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Well, so it is stated by navigators who have been in those waters.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I can show the hon. gentleman a couple of charts prepared by different engineers which might convince him that he is wrong.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
The formation at the mouth of the Nelson is similar to the formation at the mouth of the Mersey. There is a little more clay and there are more pebbles in the sand at the mouth of the Nelson, and that is an advantage; but at the same time it is a
sand formation, and wherever there are sand bars out in the open sea the channel shifts. That is the case in every part of the known wmrld. Now, that is the situation. If it takes three dredges working twenty-four hours a day and 365 days in the year to keep open the channel leading into the Mersey, a width of three-quarters of a mile, how many dredges would it take to keep the channel clear at the mouth of the Nelson river?
The Hudson Bay railway and navigation of Hudson strait and Hudson bay are different things, although they are linked up with each other. At least in some respects they may be considered separately. About a year ago, I think, a delegation came here from Manitoba, possibly from Winnipeg; and I was anxious, as I have been anxious for years, to get all the information I could upon this question. The delegation desired to meet the members of parliament in the Railway committee room and I made it a point to be present because I expected some information from the men who came from that part of the country and who had studied the question. But I was sadly disappointed.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: The delegation assumed that the government had all the information.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I do not know that any
delegation comes here that is not prepared to give to the government and to parliament all the information it can.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Surely the government
had the information before it ventured on the project.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
For that matter, I have
a good deal of information on the subject and I presume there are other members who have more than I have. And my information is in accordance with what I am stating tonight. I attended that meeting with an open mind, for I wanted to hear everything I could on the subject. But as I say, I was disappointed. Some members of the delegation quoted poetry, and all spoke eloquently; but without reflecting on any of those gentlemen, I do not think they submitted an argument. Premier Bracken, I must say, seemed to realize that it would be advisable at least to present some argument; and he did. In the course of his remarks I put this question: "If the navigation of Hudson strait and Hudson bay were shown to be impracticable from a commercial standpoint, would you still advocate the completion of the Hudson Bay railway to Port Nelson?" He hesitated; but although I cannot give his answer in his own words I think I can give the substance

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hughes
of it without doing him any injustice. He finally stated that if it could be shown, although he did not think it could be shown, that the navigation of Hudson strait and Hudson bay was impracticable from a commercial standpoint he would hesitate, for the time being at least, to recommend the extension of the railway.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: And that is the attitude of every hon. gentleman in this section of the House.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that.
But I think I shall be able to show my hon. friend that the navigation of Hudson strait and Hudson bay is impracticable and I shall quote authorities who are not prejudiced, the men whose business it was to look into this question, having been sent into these waters for the express purpose. I shall quote from the log of the Neptune, and in the first place I want to point out what kind of ship the Neptune was:
The Neptune, the largest and most powerful ship of the Newfoundland sealing fleet, was chartered as the most suitable vessel for the cruiser work. The Neptune is a stout wooden ship, built entirely of British oak, sheathed with "iron-bark" and green-heart. Although built in 1873, she is quite sound throughout, and of amazing strength. Her sides are formed of an outer sheathing of four inches of greenheart, on top of four inches of oak, covering heavy oak timbers, with an inside lining of three inches; the space between the inner and outer skins and the timbers is solidly filled with rock-salt, so that the sides of the ship are practically eighteen inches thick in all parts where a contact with the ice is expected. The bow is further reinforced by a heavy sheathing of iron plates, and inside it is backed with deadwood, giving it a thickness of eight feet.
Surely that ship could withstand great pressure from the ice; she was wtell fitted1 to test the navigation of these waters. Now, we all know that the Hudson's Bay Company's vessels navigated) these waters, if not for two hundred' years, at any rate for a very great period of time. But let os remember that these were sailing ships, stout wooden vessels, converted frigates; and time was of no great consequence to them. If they made one or two,voyages in the year, indeed if they made onle, they did well; they would bring a cargo of supplies and1 take home a cargo of furs. The drift of the ice in Hudson strait is eastward', and if these ships were going home late in the season and they got into the ioe they could afford to wait and let the ice take them into the Atlantic ocean. That is an entirely different proposition from the operation of steel ships, tramp vessels, carrying grain and cattle through these waters. As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), the cattle would have to arrive in

reasonable time, and the ships that would engage in this trade would necessarily have to make regular sailings. Time therefore would be of importance to them. I wilLcome to that later. But I wanted to make this reference to the ships of the Hudson's Bay Company that navigated these waters. Conditions to-day are absolutely different. Now we will continue with the cruise of the Neptune. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) stated that under the most favourable conditions three months in the year would be the outside limit during which these waters could be navigated. I think he was very optimistic, in fact according to the log of this ship he was incorrect even in giving that limited period, although hon. members opposite say that navigation could be successfully carried on for a much longer time. I might say that neither Hudson bay nor Hudson straits ever freeze over; I agree at once wth hon. gentlemen opposite who have made that statement. But the waters are full of floating ice every month of the year; and it is 'heavy northern ice, different altogether from the ice that is found in the gulf of St. Lawrence, the Northumberland straits or the river St. Lawrence. Here is what the log of the Neptune says in regard to Hudson bay, on September 13, the best month in the year for navigating these waters,-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: What year?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
In 1903 and 1904. This was in 1903; he was going in:
Squalls of snow delayed us until the afternoon of September 13, when we steamed westward along the north side of Digges islands. A bear was seen climbing over the cliffs^ and a boat was lowered in chase, but animal escaped. In the evening, the course was changed to northward, up Fox channel. At daylight the next morning ice was met with some ten miles from Leyson point. Steaming slowly through it, Seahorse point, on Southampton island, was reached at noon, and a landing was made with the launch.
There was ice there; that is the western end of Hudson straits.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: If my hon. friend will pardon me, this point was discussed last session, and it was then pointed out that Southampton island is not on the course to Hudson bay, it lies to the north.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I know where it lies.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
She was not coming into
Nelson if she was going by Southampton island to the north.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
We will go on.
On October 10 a heavy gale blew from the westward, accompanied by frequent, thick snow squalls.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hughes
The anchor was raised at daylight on the morning following, when, keeping well to the southward of the shoals beyond the mouth of the inlet, we arrived safely at Fullerton at dusk that evening.
He wintered in Fullerton harbour and came out next summer, 1904. He says:
The anchor was hoisted and the moorings to the ice cast off at two o'clock on the morning of July 18, when the Neptune proceeded to break her way out of Fullerton harbour, after having been nine months there fast frozen in the ice.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Was he going in to
Port Nelson, or going further north?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
He was examining these
waters to ascertain whether navigation was commercially practicable.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: If he was going further north he could not have been making for Port Nelson.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Is my hon. friend acquainted with the geography of that part of the country? If he is, he will know where Port Fullerton is situated; if not, I will tell him. Port Fullerton is on the northwest side of Hudson bay.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: But the point is-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
have a little patience.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but the Neptune could not have been in the track of vessels going to Port Nelson.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Going to Port Nelson
vessels must pass through Hudson strait. Is that established?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Very well.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: But not up Fox channel.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Now, they came out of
Fullerton harbour and they were in Hudson bay:
Beyond cape Prefontaane the ice became more plentiful-
They were steaming south now.
-and many large pans were met with. The ice had the appearance of being lately broken up, and owing to its smooth unrafted condition we judged it came from Fisher strait, rather than from Fox channel to the northward. During the night this ice forced the ship southward into the channel between Coats-
You know where that is.
-and Mansfield, so that the western shore of the latter was reached some twenty-five miles to the south of its northern end.
Open leads in the ice were found-
You get open leads in the ice.
-from three to five miles from that island, and no difficulty was experienced in gaining its north end. This island of limestone is somewhat higher than Coats and Southampton, rising inland in low broad terraces to an elevation of upwards of a hundred feet. Small patches of snow were seen under banks and along the faces of the terraces, but elsewhere the green colour showed that considerable vegetation covered the greater part of its surface. Similar lanes of water, between large cakes of ice, afforded an easy passage from Mansfield to Digges islands.
Digges island is at the entrance to Hudson strait. Now, this is on July 21:
A great amount of ice was seen to the southward, apparently completely filling the channel between Mansfield and the mainland.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: What kind of ice was it?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Hard, northern ice.
To the northward some open water occurred, but the patches became smaller and smaller as Digges was approached, and finally ceased to the eastward of these islands, the southern part of the western end of Hudson strait being completely filled with ice.
The southern part of the western end of Hudson strait being completely filled with ice on July 21, 1904.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Was the evidence which the hon. member is reading in the possession of the government between 1908 and 1910?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
What in the world has
that to do with the navigation of the straits?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
If they were in possession
of the evidence at that time why did they spend $14,000,000 and promise to complete the project?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I am not apologizing for
the government of either party; I am quoting evidence which in my opinion proves that this project is commercially impracticable.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Why didn't they give
this evidence at the proper time and so prevent this huge blunder? You were a member of the House at the time the alleged mistake was made. Do you not think you are a little bit late now?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Will my hon, friend ask
somebody else ?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Order. Members in addressing the House must speak through the Chair.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I am reminded by my
hon. friend here-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, might I
be permitted another question? I do not want to unduly interrupt the hon. member, but I should like to know whether the ice he refers to completely blocked the straits.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Hughes
He says it was over on one side. Did it necessarily interfere with the passage to the west of the straits?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend could not have been paying attention to me when I was reading this log. I am reminded by my hon. friend here (Mr. Duff) that even if a blunder was made-and I admit that-that would be no good reason why we should continue spending money in making the blunder still greater. I put that to my hon. friends opposite. I am sure they will not say that it is a good reason. I will read the sentence again:
To the northward some open water occurred, but the patches became smaller and smaller as Digges was approached, and finally ceased to the eastward of these islands, the southern part of the western end-
Now, that is the direct course for ships going into Port Nelson or coming out.
-the southern part of the western end of Hudson strait being completely filled with ice.
A strong southerly wind had been blowing all day, and it was hoped it had loosened the ice along the southern shore of the strait. The ship was taken under the land, but without success, so that after butting through the slowly closing ice all night, we were finally tightly beset in the early morning, about three miles from the eastern Digges island.
The 21st was foggy, with snow flurries in the morning and showers in the afternoon; the ice remained tight about the ship all day, and she drifted eastward with the ice, passing Cape Wolstenholme, and in the evening being about five miles to the east of Erik cove. At that time considerable open water could be seen about five miles from the ship to the eastward, with a few narrow lanes in the rear, and other small openings to the northward, where the dark sky showed considerable open water beyond our view. Persistent ramming-
Listen to this:
Persistent ramming forced the ship through about five miles of ice on the morning of the 22nd, when she was again tightly beset until the evening, at that time being about twenty-five miles to the eastward of Cape Wolstenholme, this distance having been made by the drift of the ice.
Those who are acquainted with ice navigation know that ramming ice is very trying work for a ship. Indeed, a ship must be of more than ordinary construction in order to do it at all. The ship has to back off from the ice, put on a full head of steam and ram the ice in order to make an impression upon it. No ordinary ship could think of doing that; no ship that was not specially and powerfully constructed could think of doing it. And yet these were the conditions under which this vessel tried to get through on the 22nd of July. Now, here are the conditions on September 8:
The weather throughout the morning had been bad, a strong northwest breeze bringing down frequent heavy blinding showers of snow. These showers became almost continuous, and towards noon only momentary glimpses of the land were to be obtained

at long intervals. The tides here are very swift, and when the sky cleared a strong ice-glint was to be seen ahead. It was considered dangerous to attempt to enter the ice in such weather, with the unknown Mill	islands	directly in	the course;	we	thereforeturned back to pass south of Nottingham island. This decision proved wise, for next day the whole mouth of Fox channel was found completely filled with	'heavy	ice drifted	south from	the	northern
parts of that channel. The condition of the Neptune's stem did not warrant any contact with the ice that could possibly be avoided.
The ship had been injured in the meantime, due to the efforts that were being made to get through the ice. I quote further:
On the 13th, having rounded Salisbury and Nottingham during the night, ice was met with at nine in the morning, twenty-five miles to the westward of the last-mentioned island. The course was changed to south of west to skirt the edge of this great pack, and as it continued unbroken to the westward, the idea of passing through Fisher strait was abandoned, and the course was laid to the southward of Coats island. The passage was encumbered by ice until dark, when t'he ship lay-to awaiting daylight.
Could -ordinary ships navigate in these waters under those conditions? I have only to ask tlhe question. I quote further:
The homeward voyage from Fullerton to Port Burwell was made in fine weather and the only incident requiring mention-
Sometimes you can get in and out, and sometimes you cannot.
-was that the ice from Fox channel had advanced southward and westward nearly twenty miles since we last saw it. This necessitated our keeping close to Mansfield island.
And so on. I need not read any more. It should be unnecessary to submit any further evidence.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend mind
reading the paragraph on page 39?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Yes, I will read any part
of it. This is from page 39:
The following summary of the condition and extent of the ice met with on the passage from Fullerton to Port Burwell may prove of interest and value. Large quantities of ice were encountered between the mouth of Evans strait and Digges at the western end of Hudson strait, but without serious trouble safe passages were found through it, and there is no doubt that an ordinary unprotected iron steamship would have passed through it at that time without trouble or danger.

This ice was evidently the product of the past winter, consisting chiefly, as has been mentioned, of large flat sheets that had only a short time previously broke in from the original position, for there were no signs that it had been subjected to pressure or to the action of a swell

surprised. But under the present circumstances, in view of existing conditions, with our finances standing as they do at present, and settled parts of the country requiring railway accommodation, would reasonable men undertake such a proposition? I do not think so. Will it do our western friends any good to get money expended on a project that is not practicable? All the captains and commanders who have been up in that part of the country, to whom I have spoken, have stated that if this project is undertaken at all Fort Churchill should be the terminus. I would make this proposal: That the government invite tenders from Shipping companies, people who might be in a position to tender, offering all the railway north of the Pas, all the work that .is done at Port Nelson free, asking them what bonus they would take to finish the railway, build the elevators, complete the terminals, construct the ships and carry grain and cattle to Europe.
