more money on tlhis scheme. We cannot afford it and in my opinion it would be no benefit to the east, west, middle or any other part of Canada. It would simply be throwing away more money after the large amount which has been spent already. I will therefore have to vote against the resolution.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
In common with my hon. friend from Kings P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) I do not pose as an authority on this question, but I think some of my arguments will be quite as logicial as the contentions which the hon. member has presented. In fact my hon. friend made one statement which is completely at variance with the opinions of some of the engineers who have studied this question. One of the Tyrrell brothers lived on both sides of the straits for some years. The member for Kings, P.E.I. said the ice always travelled eastward. One of the Tyrrell brothers says the two currents are maintained continuously through the straits, one going out and the other coming in, and all navigators, for the last 200 years have known that; therefore they take one going out and the other coming in, whether they have ice or not, and they are sure to keep going.
But of all the mistakes we have made regarding the trade and commerce of this country, I think there is none more glaringly outstanding than our policy in regard to a provision for the moving of our products to the markets of the world. In the construction of the three transcontinental railways which we have built, we should have turned our attention earlier to the proposition of finding a port as near as possible to the district where our products are grown. The Hudson Bay ports present a solution of our transportation problem, but now that we have the three transcontinental railways built it is not reasonable that agriculture in western Canada should be hampered by the great deficit on our National Railways and to keep the other railways solvent all these years. This project has been advocated by politicians ever since confederation. Leading statesmen such as Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir John A Macdonald advocated it many years ago; in fact, many of our politicians of late years have expressed themselves in favour of the proposal being proceeded with as a national undertaking. In a discussion of the bill of 1908, in which the Hon. Frank Oliver sought to provide for the cost of the undertaking by the sale of pre-emptions in the arid portions of the province. Sir Robert Borden, leader of the opposition at that time, declared himself in the following manner:

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Evans

If not an acre of this land is sold in the next ten years I trust and am led to believe that the Hudson Bay railway project will go on in the meantime and without delay.
I take that from the Winnipeg Free Press of January 13, 1923. Surely it cannot be forgotten by those who so vigorously opposed the completion of this road, that the cost of the whole undertaking has been provided for out of the sale of pre-emptions in that part of Canada most interested in the project. This seems to have been lost sight of by all those great champions of economy in eastern Canada. Seemingly they would prefer that all of the work and materials already used should be abandoned in the future, than that the trifling sum needed to lay the steel on the remaining portion of the grade which is completed should be spent. The Dominion Lands Act was amended by parliament at the instance of Hon. Frank Oliver in 1908, with the consent of parliament, to provide that the cost of the undertaking should be defrayed from the proceeds gained by pre-empted and purchased homesteads in the central portions of the three prairie provinces. Mr. Oliver made it plain that his purpose was to create a new source of revenue which while not adding to existing taxation burdens or constituting any additional drain on the treasury would defray the expenses of the new government railway undertaking, and at the same time encourage at a moderate cost to the settlers the settlement of these areas in the three prairie provinces, and some 28,000,000 acres in these areas were set aside for this purpose. The fact remains that these lands in the portion of Canada most interested have been sold for this purpose. It may be argued that these lands belonged to the Dominion. They did not. The lands disposed of for this purpose belonged to those provinces. If the Dominion had anything to do with them, they were simply held in trust by the Dominion, and in this case the injustice becomes all the greater.
Under the circumstances, I cannot look on it in any other light than as an act of usurpation on the part of the Dominion government. Here again, the absurdity of our present system and the danger to confederation are plainly seen. Quebec and Ontario do not want to see the Hudson Bay railway completed, and as long as these two provinces dominate the House of Commons and the Senate, they deem it safe to override the rights of the people in other parts of the country. But even admitting that no breach of the constitution has been committed, the injustice to that part of Canada which furnishes by its industry, 60 to 70 per cent of the national income yearly, becomes an out-
standing and glaring exhibition of selfishness on the part of the eastern portion of the Dominion.
Under the Land Act of 1882, it was provided that a grant of land of 6,800 acres per mile would be given to any private company that would build the Hudson Bay railway to the Saskatchewan river. From there on to Churchill or Nelson a grant of 12,800 acres per mile was offered. The act of 1908 regarding the sale of pre-emptions relieved the country of the provisions of the act of 1882. It is an accepted principle in both private and public business that if you do not pay anything, you do not say anything. Yet eastern Canada, without a dollar invested in the Hudson Bay railway is making all the protest against its construction. The settlers have purchased these pre-emptions, and the whole of the population in that area were encouraged to stay and build up the country on the assurance of the construction of that road. Any individual who buys land and pays cash therefor, if he fails to get delivery, has recourse to the courts. I ask: Has the west any recourse in this matter? I wish to say right here that those three provinces do not intend to remain as a vassal state to eastern Canada or to continue in political servitude forever. The government of Canada have already sold 126,000,000 worth of these lands. They have received nearly $20,000,000 in cash and the balance will eventually be paid to .the Dominion treasury. Surely, in the face of these facts the government cannot longer ignore the call of the west.
That there is a deficit on the present government railways cannot lbe used as an argument in refusing a road to the natural outlet of so large a section of this Dominion as the prairie provinces represent. The west expects to bear its full share of the taxes of this country. Unless the government will recognize the, right of that part of Canada, serious complications are bound to ensue.
To me the argument of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has every appearance of being dictated by the interests of Montreal and other eastern cities. In fact, the whole Hudson Bay railway project is no longer a question of its feasibility, as regards either the navigability of Hudson strait or the revenue producing possibilities of the road itself to the bay, supposing that the strait is open only for a very short period. The project since 1918 has become a part of the great injustice practised on other parts of Canada by this tariff-fed, artificially created, industrial area 'between Montreal and Windsor.
I would like to ask:	Does the Minister of

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Campbell
Agriculture or ajny of the directors of industry or finance-and I will include politics as well -of eastern Canada believe that the people of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta can be so gullible as to accept the statement that the whole project is now to be held up because someone says that in his opinion, Churchill would make the best outlet? If that engineer, McLachlan, is sure now that Nelson cannot be made a harbour, why did he work for years at Nelson and not tell us so then, but delay his opinion until the demand from the west had become'imperative? If the work was stopped in 1918 because Nelson was found to be impracticable as a harbour, why have both Liberal and Conservative governments chosen to lie down under the difficulty without trying to find an outlet in some other place?
If, as the excuse has been given, Canada cannot afford the money necessary to complete the project, why, may I ask, is the Welland canal being proceeded with? That is a project that will entail a cost of, perhaps, $100,000,000 before it is completed. The Minister of Railways and Canals has told us in this House that the Welland canal is being constructed for the sake of the west. If that is so, one-half of the yearly appropriation to the Welland canal would suffice to complete the Hudson Bay railway and terminals, and it would offset the necessity of spending $100,000,000. Surely it would be worth the trial, seeing that the Hudson Bay railway is so near completion. Besides that, let me point out the fallacy of such an argument in the fact that the Welland canal is being constructed on such a scale that it cannot be used to its capacity until another $100,000,000 is spent on locks and canals both east and west of that undertaking. Yet we are told that the country cannot afford to complete the Hudson Bay railway. I repeat:	The
whole question is one of class privilege. They say in the east too that the bay and strait are not and never will be navigable, and the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) has been very brave to-night in throwing out a challenge to us to undertake this scheme ourselves or to invite some other company to construct the road.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It was the hon. member
for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) who told me that the west would finance it themselves.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I was just wondering what
use the Hudson Bay railway would be to the farmers of western Canada without some control of the Canadian National system as it
179i
stands. To that let me reply that if the government will lay the ninety miles of steel needed and will construct wharves sufficient to facilitate the loading and unloading of boats on the Nelson, they can easily test the feasibility of this project by making Port Nelson a free trade port. We could have one free trade port for Canada, and if that were done I think the question would be settled within two years as to whether the straits are navigable or not. This surely will appeal to the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) as well. If the straits are not navigable, then the privileged interests of Montreal and Toronto surely cannot object to making Port Nelson a free trade, port. But I am convinced that unless this business is taken in some way out of reach of the directors of politics in eastern Canada the whole project will still be in danger even after the completion of the line and the terminals. Some of my statements may sound rather harsh, but speaking as one who has watdhed the shuttlecock game of all governments that have been in power since the prairies have been developed agriculturally I wish to serve notice that any party who wishes again to gain the confidence of western Canada and restore the respect in which the politics of any country should be esteemed must now drop any two-faced argument in favour of class privilege and treat westerh Canada not as a vassal of Ontario and Quebec but as an integral part of the Dominion.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I
have no intention of making a long address covering the whole ground that has been gone over before in regard to the necessity for completing the Hudson Bay railway or of its feasibility. This latter has been proved years ago. I will rather confine myself tonight to a rebuttal of the arguments that have been advanced by the opponents of the scheme.. An hon. member on the Liberal benches referred to railways built in western Canada and he interjected a question in the course of the address of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey). The implication of the question was that this government was spending a large amount of money on railway construction in western Canada. That is perhaps true, but not to the, extent implied by the question. Last year we voted $27,000,000 for railway construction work in western Canada, and $21,000,000 in eastern Canada; and I think that when we take into consideration the fact that western Canada is relatively undeveloped in comparison with
2812	COMMONS
Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Campbell
eastern Canada, the east is getting its full share of railways. And in any case, when we ask ourselves the question why these railways are being built, we must admit that they are certainly no bonus to western Canada inasmuch as we must expect to pay for them. We are assessed to pay for these railways so that they cannot possibly be considered as a bonus to us, as some of the public works and canals built in eastern Canada. The freight that will [DOT]be handled over these railways must pay the cost. And if we need more railways than we should in western Canada, it is because of past blunders on the part of previous federal governments in surveying enormous areas of land and opening up country that should not have been opened up, at least in this generation. We have sufficient surveyed land in the west to-day to accommodate 50,000,000 people. At the instance, I presume, even of land speculators, great tracts were opened up; a vast area of land was thrown open in the interests of the railway companies and land grafters. Settlers went into these lands, senit there often by the government; and in fact, when land is surveyed, that is practically an invitation to settlers to occupy it. That is the situation in western Canada to-day. But when we come to other expenditures, such as public works, which I might almost be safe in saying are a direct gift to the provinces in which they are constructed, seeing that nothing has to be paid back on account of them, as is the case with the railways, we find that from 1913 to 1923 inclusive there was spent in public works in Ontario and Quebec the sum of $98,916,000; and during the same period the same department spent only some $10,465,000 in the three prairie provinces. When these figures are fairly considered it will be seen what an undue proportion was spent in eastern Canada, while we in the west must pay our share of it.
I was rather pleased this summer when I noticed that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) had become a convert to the Hudson bay route. I had been somewhat disappointed that session after session we should get no support from the minister, and it was rather pleasing to think that he had come to the support of the project. But when he spoke on the budget some time ago I found that he indirectly opposed the Hudson bay route, so that I was rather premature in congratulating him. The minister uses as an indirect means of opposing it his opposition to the port of Nelson, and he tells us that a terrible blunder was made when Nelson was chosen instead of Fort Churchill. In that connection the Laurier government sent a 
competent engineer, Mr. R. D. Fryde, to Port Nelson, and another equally competent man, Mr. W. J. Cleaver, to Fort Churchill. When the reports of both were handed in to the Deputy Minister of Railways, Mr. Butler, who was himself an experienced engineer of recognized ability, he decided in favour of Nelson. When the Borden government came into power they somewhat doubted the wisdom of the decision and they made a new investigation; engineers were sent over the ground again, and after the reports were received, Hon. Frank* Cochrane also decided in favour of Port Nelson. Going over these reports and summing up the arguments for and against the two ports, I believe that any fair-minded observer must come to the conclusion that after all the decision in favour of Nelson was a wise one. Churchill is often described as a natural harbour, and undoubtedly it is. It is a land-locked harbour, but it is land-locked to this extent, that when the ice breaks up in the spring it is a month or six weeks longer getting out to the ocean than it is in the case of Nelson. As a matter of fact, in the spring when the ice breaks loose in the Nelson river every bit of it is gone long before the ice disappears in Churchill. And Churchill is a very small harbour; at the present time it could not accommodate more than four ocean liners, and it would take a tremendous amount of dredging at an enormous expense to enlarge it. One of the engineers points out that the dredging would be an almost impossible task owing to the fact that there are tremendous boulders that could hardly be handled at all by ordinary machinery. I think therefore that a wise decision was made when Port Nelson was chosen. I conclude therefore that the Minister of Agriculture has not given this matter intelligent study; and in opposing Nelson he is indirectly opposing the whole proposition. Now, Fort Churchill is open only for a very short time during the year. While some claim that Nelson could almost be made a winter port, Mr. Tyrrell, an engineer who did a great deal of work for the government there, points out that with a light ice-breaker ships can go in and out of Port Nelson at any period of the year. Recently I was talking to a partner of J. D. McArthur, the contractor who had a great deal to do with building the railway and the works around Port Nelson. He had spent two years there, and he told me that- there never was a time during those two winters when he would dare walk a horse across the channel of the river at the dock, and that an ordinarily heavy vessel would

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Campbell
'have very little difficulty at any time in forcing her way through the ice.
Now, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) this afternoon raised some arguments about the depth of the channel leading into Port Nelson. I have a chart here, which engineer J. W. Tyrrell very kindly sent me, drawn by himself as the result of a great deal of labour. It shows the depth every few feet from the artificial island out to the mouth of the river. At the dock the water is thirty feet deep, it averages that depth for a considerable distance, in fact that is the minimum depth until we come to what is called the "hump." It appears there is a hardpan ridge just below the dock, and over that ridge there is only twenty feet of water. Immediately after that ridge is crossed, we come into what is called the "deep hole," Where ships can ride at anchor in perfect safety in any kind of weather, according to the reports of some of these navigators and engineers. I find that in this portion called the "deep hole," the water is sixty feet deep. After that it becomes shallower until at the mouth of the river the depth is only 26 feet, but beyond it keeps getting deeper and deeper until it runs to 54 feet at the extreme mouth of the river.
I think it was also the hon. member for Brome as well as the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) who raised the question of silt or mud that would have to be continually dredged to keep the channel open. Anyone looking at the charts drawn by engineer McLachlan and engineer Tyrrell, and reading their reports, will be convinced that this is a pure fallacy. At the beginning there was a great deal of discussion as to how the deposit of mud could be overcome, because the original plan was to build a dock at the edge of the river, between that dock and the channel there would be a mud flat, and the washing of the water would continually fill up the ohannel with silt. The engineers overcame that by building an artificial island right out to the very edge of the channel. So that objection no longer holds good. Engineer Tyrrell tells me in a letter which I have received from him that the whole channel from the dock to the mouth of the river is hardpan, and he adds that owing to the speed of the current it is absolutely impossible for any silt or sand to be deposited in that channel.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: How wide is that channel?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
At the dock it is 3,000 feet, a little more than half a mile, and it keeps broadening out until at the mouth it is several miles wide. He points out that the
mean velocity of the river at the dock is eight knots per hour, and when the tide is going out it is ten and a quarter knots per hour, and that with such a speed, combined with the great volume of water, it is absolutely impossible for any silt or sand to become deposited in that channel. Therefore I think we ought to be convinced that the engineers at that time used good judgment in choosing Port Nelson instead of Fort Churchill. In this particular regard I should like to quote from an editorial in the Saskatoon Daily Star. I might point out that this is not a Conservative paper, it is not a Progressive paper, but it is a very consistent supporter of the Liberal party, and particularly of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). Yet this is what it says in its issue of April 9:
" Motherwell for Churchill terminus." So reads the most discouraging and irritating headline that has appeared in a western newspaper for many months.
After some further observations the article continues:
Thus spoke Mr. Motherwell in the House of Commons in April, 1925. The same gentleman told a different story in September, 1924. He was then in Saskatchewan and had just returned from a trip to Port Nelson. Speaking at Prince Albert, he said:
"Twenty millions have been spent on the road, and it would take about $5,000,000 to complete it to Port Nelson. It is the logical thing to go on."
Further on it quotes the minister as saying:
"It will take over a year to put the road in shape from The Pas to Kettle rapids, a distance of 332 miles. After that we will be ready to tackle the last 92 miles into Port Nelson. The time limit for completion will depend upon how our budget balances during the next session."
Then the article proceeds:
Not a word about Fort Churchill did Mr. Motherwell utter. His remarks in September, 1924, did not indicate that the place even existed. But in April, 1925, Mr. Motherwell wonders why Port Nelson was ever chosen as the terminus. Fort Churchill is the only logical choice. At any rate, the point is at least doubtful and ought to be cleared up before construction continues.
There are some further observations, not very flattering to the Minister of Agriculture, particularly when coming from a Liberal newspaper, but I will not weary the House by reading them.
Now, Engineer Cowie, Who was an employee of the Montreal Harbour Commission, has already been quoted this afternoon. He has been quoted by the press as saying that there was not a single obstacle in the development of the Hudson bay route that had not already been overcome in the St. Lawrence route. That is the word of an engineer of recognized ability living in Montreal. It raised

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Campbell
such a storm in that city that demands were made by some local newspapers for his professional head in a charger. So you can see what an engineer has to contend with in any part of eastern Canada, particularly in the city of Montreal when he dares speak the truth about such projects. I must admit that in the province of Ontario the prejudice is not so strong.
The Prime Minister-I am sorry the right hon. gentleman is not in the House, for I feel rather guilty in making these remarks in his absence-the Prime Minister in his tour of western Canada last summer spoke very hopefully of the Hudson Bay railway. He did not raise any of these objections that his colleagues are raising now. He rather gave the people the impression that he was quite in favour of it. He pointed out that the government intended to build the Hudson Bay railway just so soon as financial conditions would permit, and that when the government brought down its financial programme it took the members of its own party into its inner councils and discussed this and other matters with them. He added:	When these things
are being discussed where are our Progressive friends? Why, they are secreted off in a room by themselves. He added that the moral was plain, and he wound up 'by saying, "I ask you to think this matter over between now and the next general election". Now, what was the implication of the Prime Minister's remarks? Was it not a direct invitation to the people of western Canada to support the Liberal party and elect Liberal members, whereupon they would have a chance to secure the Hudson Bay railway? I do not like to use the word bribe, but his invitation to the people of western Canada looks very much like it. I may say to his colleagues that there are a number of hon. gentlemen in this section of the House who would probably like to attend their caucus, and I think some of us here would be glad to see them do so, for the quicker they go there the quicker we here will know where we stand. But perhaps their constituents may have something to say about that.
The hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes)-and I would just like his attention for a moment; I do not want to criticize his remarks when he is not listening-made the statement that the Hudson strait was full of very heavy ice every month in the year. Now I hardily think the hon. gentleman was serious when he said that; perhaps it was a slip of the tongue, because he dealt with the question in a very fair manner. But if, he says, the straits are full of heavy ice every

month in the year, a ship could never go in there at. all; yet ships are going in and passing through there every season.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: That is the report of the commander of the Neptune. The report will bear that out.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I understood,1 it to be the hon. member's own opinion. If I misunderstood him, I beg his pardon for it. Now, I may say that an engineer, Mr. J. W. Tyrrell, was employed by the Laurier government to go up to the straits and to investigate the situation thoroughly from the standpoint of their navigability. He moored his vessel inside the strait; according to his report, he took up a position in a rocky cavern 400 feet above the level of the sea and he spent the whole winter there. In his report, which is a very comprehensive and illuminating one -and I would commend it to the attention of the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. and also to the hon. member for Brome because I think the hon. member for Brome made the statement that the straits were not navigable for more than three weeks in the year-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Three months.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Three weeks, I think, is what the hon. member said.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: No, no, pardon me; I never said anything of the sort. What I did say was that the straits were, on the outside, not navigable for more than three months of the year.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I think the hon. member said three weeks first; probably he qualified it later on.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I said six weeks to three months. I try to be careful about what I say.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
The member for
Lunenburg said three days.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear. Quite right, and I can prove it. I will do so before I get through.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
This engineer, J. W.
Tyrrell, stated that there was no time during the whole winter that the ice was not constantly on the move, and that there were open spaces through which a vessel could pass in all except two months of the year January and February. Again with regard to Nelson, Mr. R. D. Fryde states in his report-I have the quotation here-that with a light ice-breaker Nelson could easily be kept open all winter. So I think it is unnecessary to discuss the question of feasibility or otherwise of the project. The whole question before us is whether

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. McConica
the government intend to build the railway or not. That is the whole question, and I am going to be frank and say I am quite convinced, after being four years in this House, that the government has firmly
10 p.m. made up its mind it is not going to build it, but if it can keep the project dangling before the eyes of the people of western Canada for another generation or two and thereby get a few votes, it is going to try to do so. I think the proper and commendable thing for the government to do is to come out plainly, state its position and relieve the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) of some responsibility, and some embarrassment-and say just whether or not it ever intends to build this railway.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no disposition to delay the House or to prolong this discussion. I wish however, to associate myself with those who have favoured the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. I make no pretence to personal knowledge as to its feasibility, but the people I represent are intensely interested in the building of the Hudson Bay railway. They have been taught to believe that the project is feasible; moreover, they cannot comprehend how the government should have spent $20,000.000 on a thing that is absolutely impracticable during the whole of the year except for three days, as one hon. gentleman, I think, suggested. Now, western Canada, the part of it from which I come at least, will never be satisfied until this road is completed. They will never understand where the business sense of the government is that spends $20,000,000 and then walks off and leaves the whole thing to fall into ruin and decay. It seems to me it would be the practical thing, the reasonable thing, for the government to take some substantial step this year toward the completion of the road.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking any part in this debate until I heard some of the comments made by the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes). He quoted a report to show that on the 21st of July there was ice-strong, solid, northern ice-and also in September. A year ago last summer I crossed the ocean to the Old Country. It was not through the Hudson bay; it was through the St. Lawrence; we counted thirty-seven big icebergs that we could see with the naked eye-thirty-seven in one day; and I assure you they made the atmosphere pretty cold. I have no doubt that they were big, solid, northern ice.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: What time of year was that?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
We sailed from Montreal
about the middle of July. So that ice at that time of year is evidently not confined to Hudson bay. A year ago the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff)-or was it two years ago?-had a number of photographs that he passed round in this House to show what the conditions were in 'the Hudson bay. If I had taken all the photographs of snow and ice and frost and all the things that have happened in Saskatchewan during the time I have been farming there, I could prove without doubt that it is not a fit place to live in, much less to grow anything in. We have had seasons when we never started work until the middle of May; hon. gentlemen sitting around me know that.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: When did you have the next snow after that? Did you have snow all summer?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Every month, in one year.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: All the time?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. gentleman as I go along. On the 15th of June, 1915, when the wheat was about a foot high, it was frozen down to the ground, but we had a good crop. I am not like some hon. members in this House who talk of the blackest things they can think about and forget the good ones. We had a really good crop in that year, in spite of the frost. We had a frost in July, and still we had a crop. We had frost in August-that is a common occurrence; and we had snow in September. I have seen good snowstorms in September, time after time- and, as an hon. member reminds me, some of the wheat was standing uncut at the time. We have had our crops frozen time after time. We have had snow in October that did not go away until the following srping. What do all these things prove? Nothing. In spite of them all we can live in 'Saskatchewan; we can grow big crops in Saskatchewan of the finest stuff ever grown in the world. These things do not prove anything any more than the arguments of the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., prove about the Hudson bay, in my opinion. If I wore the same kind of spectacles that the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., wears, so that everything looked blue or black, I could prove that the part of Saskatchewan from which I come is not a fit place to live in.
It is certain that, as the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica) says, this question will not die down with our people until the

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Sales
road is built to tidewater and a fair trial given to the route. This railway will be built if the people have to build it themselves. I was at the great Farmers' Convention held in my province last January. A number of farmers were discussing this question of the Hudson Bay railway and its completion, and they asked me what I thought about it. I said "Do not fool yourselves. In my opinion it will never be built as long as the east controls the situation." One man said "Do you believe that?" I said, "I do." Then he said, "We will have to do this then. During the war we raised a lot of money for what we called a patriotic acre fund. We each gave one acre of wheat to that fund and we sent forward train loads of flour. Now, what would be the matter with doing the same thing in order to finish the Hudson Bay railroad?" I said, "You will get it built a good deal quicker if you do that than if you wait for the east to build it for you, in my opinion." I pointed out to them that one-half of one per cent-they are used to that being taken as shrinkage when they ship grain through the elevators-on a crop of 300,000,000 bushels at $1 a bushel would give SI,500,000 and at S1.50 a bushel would give $2,500,000, to say nothing of barley, oats, cattle, hogs, butter, and eggs, all of which would be shipped by this route if it proved feasible. I want to say to this House that if our people get hold of an idea like that they will surely bring it to a successful conclusion. May I appeal to our friends in the east. The Prime Minister made an appeal to us the other day to be fair to the rest of Canada. May we not appeal to gentlemen all over the rest of Canada to be fair to the west. Why not go a little further? Having spent so much money, having so much material lying idle at tide water as we hear time and again, having enough rails lying in the sidings to practically finish the road, without spending much more money for material, why not go a little further and reach tide water and prove whether this route is feasible or not? If it is not we will have to forget it. I would also like to say this to the members of the House: The idea is prevalent among many people in the west that if our friends who oppose this road so strenuously were absolutely sure that it would be a failure it would have been built years ago. But they really are afraid it will prove a success. That is why they are so determined to stop the road from reaching tide water so long as they possibly can. Now that idea is being held in the west, and the prevalence of ideas of this kind among the people there does not make for good feeling and unity in 
a country like this. Therefore I hope hon. members will give this project their serious consideration and support.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me at the very outset say that I am of the opinion that this great national project has gone altogether too far, and the national honour is entirely too much at stake, to even suggest that we repudiate the undertaking at this particular stage. If, when British Columbia entered confederation under a promise to be connected with the rest of Canada by a great transcontinental railway, Canada had repudiated the obligation what would that province have thought of it? At the time the Maritimes entered confederation the promise was made that the Intercolonial railway would be constructed. If Canada had defaulted then what would the Maritimes have thought of that failure on Canada's part to live up to its promise? And so with the present undertaking begun by a Liberal government, and carried out later by a Conservative government, and the leader of every party in Canada pledged to it, is it an enterprise that we should now talk of abandoning when 80 per cent of the road is constructed? It seems to me that would be an amazing proposal?
Now then a word or two, because I have a few more things to say, with respect to one or two members on the Progressive side. I think I am just as strong an advocate of the Hudson Bay railway as they are, and I am just as strong an opponent of Port Nelson as anybody on this side can be. They think such an attitude is contradictory; they cannot conceive of a person having different views regarding the same project without being inspired with the desire of deliberately blocking it. What would my hon. friends have said of the difference of opinion among the authorities at the time of the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway when that line was built?-some being in favour of the Pine river pass and some in favour of the Kicking Horse pass. As a matter of fact it was switched from one to the other after the road was begun. But what would have been said at the time if one side was charged by the other with blocking the enterprise because they differed as to a certain pass through which the line should run? What would1 have been thought of some of the great leaders in the world war because they differed as to the tactics to be employed in the field if such a view as that prevailed? Why the great generals would have been charging each other with un-

Hvdson Bay Ry.-Mr. Motherwell
fairness and disloyalty to the common cause. Men who have exactly the same objective but think that a different course should be taken can surely disagree as to the procedure. It is not the way to get results to upbraid each other because one man differs from another as to the procedure to be employed.
I think there are only two hon. members on the Progressive side who have adopted such an attitude, and I want to thank all the rest for not following their example. I did not hear what the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) said but as he is a decent sort I am going to assume that he did not say what the other two hon. members to whom I have referred did. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) acting true to form, threw out suggestions that my motives were not sincere. Well, I do not know how much I am going to be. hurt by that sort of insinuation. At all events I am going to take the risk of any hurt that may come to me and let it go at that. I cannot, however, refrain from remarking that any member who is always suspecting and impugning the motives of others had better be careful that he is not guilty of the very thing he is charging others with.
As to the quotation from the Saskatoon Star it is substantially correct. When I was up in that country last season, that is in 1924, I ventured as far as Kettle rapids but regretted very much, as I explained the other day in the budget debate, that I could not get further. I gave the reason why. That should have been a sufficient explanation. Everywhere I went I heard from the trapper, the miner, the engineer, and they were all amazed at Port Nelson being selected. It set me thinking but not sufficiently to make me change my mind regarding the choice of Nelson. I thought it was natural perversity on the part of some people when the government was giving them a certain thing to want something else-we see that sometimes. I still tried to believe in Nelson because I wanted to believe in that harbour; I knew that we would wTaste a lot of money if the line was not completed to Nelson; and desiring to believe in Nelson I came back. I may have made a mistake in saying anything. On my return I noticed that the other gentlemen who came back from the bay, the most of them from Manitoba, did not say very much. Still it was difficult to return through the northern part of the province of Saskatchewan without giving some impressions of your trip north, and I gave them. At that stage of the game I had not sufficient information to warrant me in throwing any doubt upon the feasibility of Port Nelson. On returning I came down the St. Lawrence, and upon reaching Ottawa I proceeded to look into the matter further. I gave the evidence which confirmed the opinion I was beginning to form, and nobody has challenged that evidence. Even (the hon. gentlemen who have imputed motives to me have nothing to say against it. If that is the case then their case is very weak indeed. The evidence upon, which I based my opinion was taken from the records of those who were supposed to know the facts, navigators and mariners such as Captain Bernier and others.
I perhaps made the mistake of the medical man who arrived at his diagnosis after only half an examination; then after the second half of the examination found the diagnosis had to be changed.

speechtext:
Does the minister mean to
say that the governments who started the work at Nelson and afterwards carried it on there did not have before them the same evidence to which he alludes?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: That means it would cost more.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Yes. Nobody can tell what it will cost. What it has cost in the past is no criterion of what it will cost, because of the shifting nature of the channel. I do not think Mr. McLachlan has changed his. views in that regard.
That is as far as I go with Mr. McLachlan1. Now we have a Hudson bay explorer and navigator by the name of Freakley. At page 38 he says:
Nelson is	not	a natural	harbour but	an open
roadstead.	[DOT]
Hon. gentlemen from the Maritime provinces might	tell	me	what that	means.
Captain Freakley continues:
The vessel	lies	in the	river	about one and	a quartermiles from	the	shore	and	the freight is	lightered
to the land.
One is a natural harbour and the other is artificial.
We have had some experience in building artificial harbours in this country. We have some harbours. Great mistakes have been perpetrated apparently on account of mistaken advice by engineers. I have every respect for engineers, but have more respect for

navigators. I refer to that famous pier in Halifax. I do not think there is a finer harbour in the world than Halifax, and yet a great blunder was committed in regard to the construction of a certain pier. We have another such harbour-I almost hesitate to refer to it-the outer harbour at Victoria- just a parallel to the one at Halifax, and all kinds of money thrown away on it. It was done precipitately and in a hurry. Are we going to repeat all this performance in the face of the statements I have quoted?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Does the minister say this has been done in a hurry?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: Yes, so far as Nelson harbour is concerned, as I will show very soon.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: This matter has been pending since 1910..

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I refer to the switching through there and the various steps that have been taken, I say if these other illustrations which I have given are bad, this is ten times worse as a 'harbour proposition. Now what are some of,the requisites of a harbour? Hon. members will pardon me if I make some mistakes in this matter, because I have lived inland all my life and have not had an opportunity of scenting the salt sea breezes very much, but from what I have read, I think we should have enough land and enough water to build a harbour. Now have we enough of either? In the case of Nelson we would1 have to build 'away out into the water, over half a mile, erect an artificial island for a harbour and put elevators on it. We are asked to build! a harbour, with all the other risks in. volved. We must deliberately take the risk of not having enough land to start with, and certainly not enough water. The water there is shallow and low, and then we have all those sand bars to contend with. Surely it does not take a mariner to understand that you must have abundance of both these essential requisites, water and land, tio build a harbour. What does a harbour mean? Does it not mean a sheltered place for ships at anchor? Where is the shelter here? Leave the other requisites cut of consideration and where is the shelter? Then there is a shortage of land. We would have to build an artificial island. It could foe done; it has -been done and it can be done again, if you like to put money into it, but how about the question of water? Shipping is only an indifferent proposition if you have not the water. In addition to the water you require a place to shelter the shipping. Where is the shelter here? Does anybody pretend

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Motherwell
there is any natural shelter? Is it a landlocked harbour? Does it resemble Prince Rupert, one of the finest harbours? Is it surrounded by any conditions to make it a landlocked harbour or anything of that kind? I do not see anything on the maps or nobody has shown me anything to indicate that it is a natural harbour. There is nothing there to constitute a shelter any more than the morning mist could be said to provide a shelter. The most important requisite for a harbour is shelter, where ships are anchored, not only to discharge their cargo, but for the purpose of getting out of the storm. I do not know where there is any place to get out of a storm at Nelson. I have been <on the prairie nearly all my life, and I think I see myself hunching up against the storm, with nothing to shelter me beyond what they have at Nelson. I would not be comfortable for the night.
Then again, while wTe are dhort of land at Nelson, short of water ajid short of shelter, we are long on dredging. I have given you all these facts; now need I go any further into it? Just think of it, with the Nelson pouring down its waters and sludge for the last century, and it will continue to do so for centuries to come, pouring out water and sludge and meeting the tides from the ocean. There is a place there-shall we call it the dead centre? There is bound to be an enormous quantity of precipitation there. Our own judgment will tell those of us who know anything in particular about the Saskatchewan river that that channel will be shifting, perhaps not every year, 'but almost every year. In face of that, if you want to make a job for dredges-and anybody who ever saw government dredges at work knows that it takes veTy little to keep them going sometimes; they go pretty slowly to my mind, at all events-there you have it from now until the crack of doom. I do not see how you are going to get away from that, and yet hon. merhbcrs upbraid me for mentioning these things. If we make the mistake of not going to this natural port, the project is all off in our life-time. I want to see it white I live and I do not want to take a step that will lead in the wrong direction. We shall have to take risks, but there is no need to take the ghastly ridk associated with Port Nelson. If anyone wishes to criticize me, let him criticize me on these facts and not on my alleged motives. I think I have as much right to be credited with being sincere as anyone else in this, and I do not see why this should be otherwise. My whole life has been spent in the west and I expect to spend the balance of it there after I get through here.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: What are those alleged motives?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It is not worth while repeating them. I just referred to them a little while ago. It is pretty hard to put the X-ray on any hon. gentleman and to tell what his motives are, and I do not care to repeat them. I will tell my hon. friend afterwards. Let me go further. This is what Captain Bernier says regarding Churchill:
I should prefer Fort Churchill, because a ship can come in and she is in a harbour. In Nelson, you have to anchor away out; before you get a chance to come in you have to contend with all that danger. Suppose you dredge there and next spring is an exceptionally fine spring and there is a heavy thaw. Your channel is filled up with sand and the channel is somewhere else. The work that you have done is lost. At Churchill you have a big body of water. Of course, some dredging would have to be done. It is land-locked. There (indicating Fort Churchill on the map) is the work of nature, and when a man has to work against nature there is no money in it.
We have evidence as regards artificial harbours, but as Captain Bernier says in his evidence before the Royal Grain Commission, Canada is too poor to keep up a port like that. Does any lover of the Hudson bay project wish deliberately to shut his eyes and blunder into Nelson with these incontrovertible facts before him? I do not agree with all that the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) or the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) say, but the sticker, especially with the hon. member for Kings, was Nelson. He knows what a harbour is; he lives by the sea, and he took some of the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite to prove that Nelson, in his estimation is, on that evidence, no good. Consequently, the great difficulty, in my opinion, in persuading eastern Canada that we should go ahead with this project is the impossibility of Nelson as a practical harbour. What is the use of going there if we are going to run into a lane with no gate at the end of it? I do not agree at all with the deductions of the hon. member for Brome. He took the ground that he did not think the Hudson bay would be open for more than three months at the most. He suggested from six weeks to three months. Captain Bernier takes the ground that it will be open for four months, and he has given in evidence that if you have radio, with all possible aids to navigation and with 10 per cent, if you like, added to the cost of construction of the ships by having proper plating, there is no doubt the time will be extended to four and one-half months. The statement has been made in the eastern press, not with any desire to mislead, but simply because they do not know anything about the matter,

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Motherwell
that you cannot get the grain out the same year it is grown. That is the very year you will get it out. If they took the ground that it is not practicable to store grain there because you might have to wait until July of the next year, there might be some justification for that. But if you will investigate when our wheat starts to move from Montreal, you will find that it is about the 1st September or the last day of August. Our wheat will be moving from Port Nelson or Fort Churchill, whichever port is constructed, as soon as it will be moving from Fort William and ten days before it will be moving from Montreal as it has a thousand miles further to go to get to Montreal. Consequently, the movement of the grain that is grown the same year will start from either Port Nelson or Fort Churchill, whichever one is finally chosen, ten days before the grain will start across the Atlantic from Montreal. How much longer is Montreal open in the fall than either of those harbours? The most that is suggested is about a month and ten days. Some suggest that it is not safe to operate Hudson strait later than the 1st November. Captain Bernier, in his evidence, said the middle of November, and if we take the latter date, it will be closed about twenty-five days earlier than Montreal will be closed. If you deduct from that the ten days, that leaves fifteen days, so that you have only about fifteen days longer to transport our wheat from Montreal than from Hudson bay in the same year in which the wheat is grown.
On the other hand, I do not look forward to its being as good a storage place for grain over winter as the grain storage such as we have at Fort William. There is no doubt that some grain will have to be kept in storage there until the following July or the first of August, and that is where the long storage and interest charges will come in. But if we can get a quantity of our wheat out in the same year as it is grown, that is going to help the peak load when the grain is rushing to Buffalo, Montreal and Vancouver. That is the time when this outlet will be most required,- and not in the spring of the year. The other routes can easily take care of the wheat in the spring of the year; but if we go on developing as' we may and should develop, we should produce sufficient cargoes to keep the Hudson bay route going at full capacity, without taking away a bushel from Montreal, or Buffalo or Vancouver. Every railway that I have seen developed in the west during the last forty years has invariably produced its own tonnage. It 
caused so much additional development that before the road or outlet was completed, enough additional settlement and development had taken .place to produce freight for the new outlet and the new line. That has been our experience with the Canadian Pacific, Grand Trunk, Canadian Northern and all the other lines that have been built in that country. They have produced their own freight. I do not know to what extent the suggestion of the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) is warranted, that it is the fear that this route will 'be a success that is actuating some people in opposition to it. Let me say to all such that the way to develop all our ports is to develop the country tributary to them. The great bulk of the grain, in my opinion, for many years will come down eastern routes, either by Buffalo, or by the Welland canal when it is completed, because there is no doubt, in that event, the attraction will .be more and more for Montreal. But before that is brought about, a great deal more storage accommodation must be provided at Montreal, or Port Col-borne, or Brockville, or Prescott, or wherever the transfer is at the present time. There is twice as much grain elevator storage at Buffalo as there is at Montreal.
So far as the right time in the matter is concerned-that is the substance of the resolution-I have nothing to say. As to when the road should be built, I do not know what the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will have to say on that point, but naturally he wil. speak for the government. I am merely dealing with the practicability of the route, leaving the matter of time, which is the essence of the resolution, to the Minister of Railways. You will remember that this great project was first undertaken by the Liberal government under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was reported as saying that while there might be some question about the practicability of the Hudson bay route it was the price we had to pay for a united Canada. And has not many a thing been done towards that great end? The price of united Canada was paid in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway, which had just as much an elfement of doubt as to its future success as exists in relation to the Hudson Bay railway to-day. Did you ever hear of any great project that has been undertaken at anv time, whether it be the Suez canal, the Panama canal, the Canadian Pacific railway or any other great enterprise, in regard to which there were not many people who were in honest doubt concerning its success? And so it is with this.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Motherwell
I am not going to upbraid my Liberal friends from the east for holding different views, although what they get is naturally coloured a little with eastern sentiment. Some of them have pretty sound views on marine matters generally, and if they take the evidence in regard to Nelson they are only coming to the same conclusions which I, a western man, have reached so far as that particular port is concerned. I understand that a deputation is on its way to Ottawa now, and in the main I think they are doing useful educational work in the furtherance of the project. But I would advise them not to be quarrelling with everybody if they want to get anywhere. When they find some of their friends holding different views from their own as to the way to attain the object in view they must not be inclined to quarrel. I say without any equivocation that to go to the wrong port at this stage would be fatal. There is no reason why there should be any delay about making a further investigation. There is more than a year's work ahead before we can reconstruct the work to Kettle rapids. There is a tremendous amount of construction work to be done also along the way not only on the road itself but on the telegraph line from mile 214 to Kettle rapids, a distance of 116 miles, and that must be done concurrently with the reconstruction that takes place. If it is desired, a further investigation can be made as to the respective merits of Churchill and Nelson, and if that investigation confirms Nelson then there is nothing for it but to go there.
But have we no additional information recently at all? Well, I remember hearing of the storm that took place a short while ago and I thought at the time that it was only propaganda; for I had been just as suspicious as any hon. member on the Progressive side regarding every move in connection with this undertaking, and when I saw that news despatch in the papers across the country I thought to myself that it was more propaganda. But I did the report injustice because there was a serious storm; and while I will not go into any of the detail's-there was nothing harowing about the information to hand in March-I know that some of the more recent reports are rather disconcerting. At any rate there was a storm and the dredges and ships mustered in that so-called harbour were torn from their moorings. I do not know where, they went but they are being rounded up now anyway. Is that a harbour? I thought a harbour was a sheltered place for shipping, but of course Nelson is not yet finished; there has been only some $6,000,000
spent on it so far. But I am told that all the evidence goes to show that Churchill is better in a state of nature than Nelson is now or can be.
There is another feature about the matter which we might well ponder, and that is that the present undertaking at Nelson, that is to say, the building of a trestle away out to the artificial island, is not the first step that has been taken; the first step was to construct a lock inland and draw the water into it. A large sum of money was spent towards that end, but it was found that it would be better to build this trestle outstream than to try to get the water into this dock. So that there has been a change of views in this regard; they can now.see some way of getting out +o the channel. But for the life of me I do not know how they are going to keep the channel in its place.
I will not dwell on this point, but I do want to urge this question. Is it not a matter of national honour at this stage to push forward with the reconstruction work to Kettle rapids having regard to what has already been done? As the hon. member for Kings indicated it would mean a tremendous lot to us if we could get to Churchill'-and that is where we shall-get-and it proves successful. You cannot describe what it will mean to the west. Is it worth while trying? Is it any greater risk trying that than there has been in connection with any other great project? I do not believe it is; and with the road 80 per cent built it would be a huge blunder to turn back. "No man having put his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom." That is what this would amdunt to, figuratively speaking at all events.
I have not said anything about aids to navigation. I have crossed the Atlantic only once but I have seen icebergs, and if the pilot had been so inclined we might have butted into them at any time, for there are scores of them in the north Atlantic. But does that say that we could not cross the Atlantic? We have heard of the Titanic going down, but surely they did not go deliberately head-on into an iceberg. And because the Titanic went down is that any argument in condemnation of the Atlantic? Not at all. With the marvels that have been attained through the radio, and with all the various fog signals and lighthouses that exist to-day, navigation is fairly safe. Look at the equipment on the St. Lawrence. I was at Prescott this winter where I saw a large building devoted to the manufacture of equipment used along the St. Lawrence route, and it was wonderful. So that there is no comparison between what can be accomplished to-day, even in dangerous

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Motherwell
seas, with what was done a few years ago. The man at the wheel and the pilot are constantly within earshot of the voice of danger, and by means of modern equipment they know just where the ice is; and they are not going to butt their heads deliberately against any iceberg, or run carelessly into any other danger.
In conclusion, my suggestion is this:	We
must reconstruct the road as rapidly as possible to Kettle rapids, because no road will ever stand still; if it is not constantly repaired it will rot. And certainly this road will not remain as it was six years ago; it is in process of disintegration continually. If we only spend a few thousand dollars every year on it we might do that for a century and get nowhere, because the work will be deteriorating as rapidly as we can repair it. We should therefore at least go as far as Kettle rapids, our resources permitting, making it possible to connect with mile 214; and we should see to the reconstruction of the telegraph lines which are pretty well dilapidated, as well as to the restoration of the road, which has been heaved up by the action of the frost where the water accumulates. Well, this is being done. There is no occasion for delay, as my hon. friends from Saskatoon and Mackenzie suggested. If it is desired that further money shall be secured for that purpose, concurrently with reconstruction of the road to Kettle rapids the investigation could be undertaken. It has often occurred to me, Mr. Speaker, why what I am going to suggest has never been done. Would it not have been the logical thing-I do not want to upbraid those who have preceded me, but it seems to me, as every farmer knows, that there is nothing like trying your plough or your binder in the field under field conditions before passing judgment on it-would it not have been the logical thing, and comparatively easy, to load up one or two Atlantic liners, or as large boats as could in safety navigate these comparatively unknown waters, with wheat, take the cargo up the Labrador coast, through the straits and, if you like, on to Fort Churchill, and, further, if you like, see how close you could get to Port Nelson, and then see how long it would take to reach Liverpool? Would that be a foolish thing to do? I cannot think so. Please do not rise up in holy indignation at the thought of something being done to make a little surer than it is to-day whether we were right in going to Port Nelson. Surely this is a case where "safety first" should to some extent determine our further action, where we should look carefully before we leap, in order that we do not jeopardize the whole 
enterprise by a mistaken step at this time, particularly when this investigational work can be undertaken concurrently with the construction of the last 116 miles of the road.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when I listened to the speech of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) on the budget, in which he threw doubt upon Port Nelson as the proper terminus of the Hudson Bay railway, I experienced a great deal of disappointment, particularly as I had just returned 'rom a very largely attended meeting at Winnipeg called under the auspicies of the On-to-the-Bay Association. Any person who attended that meeting would certainly be impressed by the strength of feeling that prevails in the city of Winnipeg in favour of the Hudson Bay railway. I repeat, I was disappointed when I listened to the Minister of Agriculture, because at that meeting Port Nelson was spoken of with great commendation and in no uncertain terms, as I judged, by men who were in a position to speak with knowledge and authority on the subject of which port should be the terminus. I did not attribute any such motives to the hon. minister as some have seen fit to do; I had no thought of attributing to him any ulterior motives whatever. Indeed, I felt that probably he was speaking his own sincere convictions in the matter. None the less, I did feel that he was making a mistake at the time, and I think he will not accuse me of being unfair, of charging against him anything I should not charge, when I intimate that he might have made a mistake in throwing doubts upon the selection of Port Nelson as the terminus of this railway.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: I might have made a political mistake, I agree. I often do that.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
I am not speaking of a
political mistake, but a mistake from the standpoint of securing completion of the road at the earliest possible date. I think it was a mistake, not that I would be disposed to criticize very severely the comparisons that have been made between Port Nelson and Fort Churchill in their natural state. Indeed, for many years I was disposed to think, as the hon. minister has expressed it, that Fort Churchill was by all odds the most suitable port in its natural state. However, we have to consider the question now, not with those ports as they were twenty years ago, but in their present state; and in view of the fact that a large development has taken place at Port Nelson, that steel has been laid within ninety odd miles of that port that the grade

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Broivn
is constructed for the remainder of the way, and that a comparatively small amount of money would be sufficient to lay the rails and perhaps subject the road to an actual test, it did seem to me that the minister was making a mistake in introducing at this particular time '**he question of the relative merits of Fort Churchill and Port Nelson. From charts I saw exhibited at Winnipeg a few weeks ago, I judge it would require the construction of a good many extra miles of railway to reach Fort Churchill. I am not certain at what point the branch-off to Fort Churchill would leave the existing grade, but I think probably it would mean the construction of at least another 150 miles of new line.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext: About 100 miles.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. KNOX FOR RECOGNITION OF PRIORITY
speechtext:
It was shown also that the line would need to be constructed over a high ridge, involving a heavy grade to reach the top of the watershed, of course running down after that point into Fort Churchill; whereas the existing grade runs along the side of the Nelson river and is down grade all the way. For these reasons I felt it was a mistake on the part of the minister to introduce at this particular time doubts regarding the feasibility of Port Nelson as the terminus. After I came back from my Easter holidays I began to hear the people were imputing motives to the minister, but it had never occurred to me that there were any other motives than simply his desire to express his own personal convictions in the matter; but, as I say, I did feel that he had made a blunder in introducing these doubts at the present time.
I believe that a comparatively small amount of money will suffice to lay rails on the existing grades, and with the development that has already taken place at Port Nelson the road could be put into a position where a test could be made, and so demonstrate beyond any manner of doubt whether it could become a commercial proposition or not. I think we cannot urge too strongly the desirability of doing this for the sake of allaying the feeling of unrest and irritation that prevails in the western provinces. There is no question that that feeling does prevail there, and undoubtedly there has been some reason for it. The prairie provinces consider -and I think myself they have a right to consider-that they have been regarded by the east as proper subjects of exploitation. We have been deprived of our natural resources; we have been regarded as the milch cow of the Dominion; the manufacturers of the east have considered us their legitimate market, which they must hold to the exclusion of all other competitors; the fruit growers of British Columbia have also considered us their natural market; and so from both sides we have been treated as though we were legitimate subjects of exploitation, and naturally we have become somewhat restive about it.
As has been well said, we are marooned in the centre of the continent, and the question of freight rates is to us one of prime importance-of infinitely more importance to us than it is to others living in any other section of the Dominion, for, remember, we must pay the rates. The conditions are such that the price we receive for our produce is the price on the world market minus the freight rates, and the price we pay for the goods we buy is the price plus the freight rates. So that when Mr. J. L. Payne in his pamphlet recently published made a comparison between the rates we were paying on our wheat and the rates that were being paid on goods shipped to the west, he was altogether aside from the mark. We pay the rates under any circumstances; the price is minus freight rates when we sell our produce and is plus freight rates when we have anything to buy. Sc that the matter of freight rates is to us infinitely more important than it is to those situated in any other part of the Dominion. It would be worth while to build this road if only to allay that feeling of irritation. It pains me, Mr. Speaker, even to hear the word " secession ". As a native born Canadian my whole nature revolts from the idea I think it is absolutely impracticable; I think those who suggest it have not taken intc consideration at all what it would mean or what would be necessary to accomplish it; I think they are thoughtless in expressing sentiments in favour of such a step. Nevertheless such sentiments are expressed, although for my part I should do everything in my power to oppose any movement in that direction. But is it not well that the people of Canada should begin to get down to solid thinking and see just what are the causes of that feeling? Why does that feeling exist in the west? For the most part it is justified, because we have been exploited on the one hand and we are denied what is our right in seeking this short outlet to the sea. It may be wrong; we may be wrong, but it would be worth the expenditure of that money, it would be worth all it would cost to build the road, to allay that feeling of irritation and bring about a better sentiment in all parts of Canada so far as the attitude of different sections toward each other is concerned.

Hudson Bay Ry.-Mr. Leader
I have very little to say in regard to the feasibility of the route, or the navigability of Hudson bay and straits. There is such an immense amount of conflicting evidence in the matter that it seems to me almost presumption for any man, unless he is a skilled navigator, to stand up in this House and express positive opinions one way or the other. But I believe that with a comparatively small expenditure the line can be put in such shape as to give the route a practical test that will settle the matter for all time.
There are some things, however, that we cannot help thinking about in forming opinions on the subject. The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), dealing with the question of national defence, referred to the fact that we needed to be defended upon the Pacific coast and uipon the Atlantic coast and suggested that there was no fear of our being attacked from the north. But there is a little incident in Canadian history that throws 6ome light on this matter. The fact is that at one time Canada was attacked1 from the north. At one time the British authorities considered it necessary to -build a great fort, Fort Prince of Wales, at Fort Churchill. Why did the British -build a fort there? Because they were afraid their then enemies, now friends, the people who come from the province of Quebec, would) attack them in that northern country at a point which was then considered vulnerable. That they were wise in their decision was proved when the French did attack Fort Prince of Wales, and the fort is now in rui-ns. It has always seemed1 to me that the British authorities of that day
11. p.m. would) never have thought of building a fort as Fort Prince of Wales did they not think there was a possibility of the enemy coming in through Hudson straits. If that could be done under the conditions that prevailed during the eighteenth century it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that it might be done in the twentieth.
We can sometimes judge of the worthiness of a cause by the enemies who array themselves against it. Man is known not -only by the company he keeps but sometimes by the character of his enemies. Who are opposed to this route? Well, we find that the opposition is centered very largely around the city of Montreal. There are certain straws which show which way the wind blows, and they indicate that such interests as the Hudson's Bay Company, the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Montreal Harbour Commissioners are opposed to the opening up of the Hudson bay route. Indeed I think there is good ground for be-
lieving that it is the fear on the part of these interests that the route would ultimately be successful that actuates their -opposition to it. I do not impute that to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster); I know he entered his protest. But the hon. member for Brome knows that these considerations do at times influence the opposition to or the advocacy of any particular interest or enterprise. The fact that this route is opposed by these interests would seem to indicate the possibility that the road is perfectly feasible.
There was a time when Montreal opposed the opening of the prairie country. One needs only to read the history of the northwest and of the Selkirk set-tiers to find out what intense opposition was offered to Lord Selkirk's scheme owing to the fact that Montreal interests wanted to keep that great land as a fur trading land and therefore to exclude settlers. If these principles governed the keen commercial men of Montreal a hundred years ago, we may perhaps be excused for thinking that the same considerations enter into their opposition to this scheme to-day.

I have great respect for the member for Kings, P.E.I.; I think he would be entirely unprejudiced in the matter. The hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. and the hon. member for Brome are two members on the opposite side for whom I have high esteem; we stand very close together in opinion in regard to a great many matters.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to associate myself very heartily with those who support this project. I know it is a project that is very dear to the hearts of the people of the west; in fact, I have no hesitation in saying that to them it is almost a matter of religious faith. Besides, there are abundant reasons for believing that the road is commercially feasible and that in time the straits will be navigated and the Hudson bay route will become one of the great trade routes of the world.
